title: React
tagline: From JSX and hooks to performance, testing, React 19 and real projects: React from scratch to hero.
description: A complete React revision track that starts with components, props, state and JSX, moves through hooks, patterns, forms, data fetching, routing, state management and styling, then covers performance, testing, React 18/19 features, TypeScript and production deployment. It ends with 15 runnable mini projects and interview questions. Most examples run live in the browser; library-heavy code (Router, Redux, TanStack Query, Next.js) is shown as text with explanations.

topics.title: What is React and Why Use It?
topics.summary: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces out of small, reusable components.
topics.description:
React is a JavaScript **library** created at Facebook (now Meta) for building user interfaces. It does one job very well: it keeps what the user sees on screen in sync with your data. You describe *what the UI should look like* for a given state, and React figures out *how* to update the real DOM.

### Why developers choose React

- **Declarative UI** - you write `UI = f(state)`. Change the state, and React re-renders. You never manually call `document.getElementById(...).textContent = ...`.
- **Component-based** - a page is a tree of small, isolated, reusable pieces (Navbar, Card, Button).
- **Learn once, write anywhere** - the same ideas power React DOM (web), React Native (mobile) and server rendering.
- **Huge ecosystem** - routing, state management, forms, testing and meta-frameworks like Next.js.
- **Unidirectional data flow** - data goes down via props, events go up via callbacks. This makes bugs easier to trace.

### Library vs framework

React only handles the view layer. Routing, data fetching and global state are separate choices. Angular and Vue (full) are more "batteries included"; React is more "bring your own".

### Imperative vs declarative

Plain JS: "find the element, change its text, add a class, remove it later". React: "when `count` is 3, show `Count: 3`". The second style scales much better as an app grows.

interview.q: Is React a library or a framework?
interview.a: A library focused on the view layer. Routing, data fetching and state management come from other libraries or from a framework built on React such as Next.js.

interview.a: You describe what the UI should look like for the current state and React handles the DOM updates, instead of writing step-by-step DOM instructions.

topics.title: Virtual DOM and Reconciliation
topics.summary: React compares a lightweight tree of the new UI with the previous one and updates only what changed in the real DOM.
topics.description:
The **Virtual DOM** is a plain JavaScript object tree that describes the UI. Every time state changes, React calls your component functions again and produces a *new* tree of React elements. It then compares that new tree with the previous one. This comparison is called **reconciliation** (the "diffing" algorithm).

### How it works

1. State or props change, so React **renders** the component (calls the function).
2. React builds a new element tree.
3. React **diffs** the new tree against the old tree.
4. React **commits** only the minimal set of changes to the real DOM.

### Diffing rules (heuristics)

- Elements of **different types** (`<div>` vs `<span>`) - React tears down the old subtree and builds a new one, losing its state.
- Elements of the **same type** - React keeps the DOM node and only updates changed attributes.
- Lists use **keys** to match old and new children, so items can be moved instead of recreated.

### Is the Virtual DOM "fast"?

It is not magic. Touching the real DOM is expensive, so React batches updates and applies the smallest diff. The real benefit is that you get a simple programming model (re-render everything conceptually) with good enough performance.

### Render vs commit

*Render* is pure calculation (no DOM touched). *Commit* is when the DOM is updated and effects run. Keeping render pure is why React rules like "do not mutate state" exist.

interview.a: The process where React compares the new element tree with the previous one and works out the minimum DOM operations to make the page match.

interview.q: Why does React need keys in lists?
interview.a: Keys give each item a stable identity so reconciliation can match, move or remove the right items instead of re-creating everything or mixing up state.

topics.title: Setting Up a React Project with Vite
topics.summary: Create a fast modern React app with Vite instead of the deprecated Create React App.
topics.description:
**Vite** is the recommended build tool for plain React single-page apps. It serves your code with native ES modules in development (instant start, fast hot reload) and bundles with Rollup for production. Create React App is deprecated, so new projects should use Vite or a framework such as Next.js.

### Requirements

You need **Node.js** (LTS) and a package manager (`npm`, `pnpm` or `yarn`). Check with `node -v`.

### Steps

1. Scaffold the project with the `react` or `react-ts` template.
2. Install dependencies.
3. Start the dev server (usually `http://localhost:5173`).
4. Build for production with `npm run build` and preview with `npm run preview`.

### Useful scripts

| Script | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run dev` | Dev server with Hot Module Replacement |
| `npm run build` | Optimized production build in `dist/` |
| `npm run preview` | Serve the built `dist/` locally |
| `npm run lint` | Run ESLint |

### Why Vite is fast

Dev mode does not bundle the whole app. The browser requests modules on demand and Vite transforms them with esbuild. Edits update only the changed module through HMR, keeping component state.

Dev server starts instantly using native ES modules
Production build goes to dist/ via Rollup
Create React App is deprecated
Env variables must start with VITE_ to be exposed

interview.q: Why prefer Vite over Create React App?
interview.a: Vite starts instantly, has fast HMR, produces optimized Rollup builds and is actively maintained, whereas CRA is deprecated and slow on large apps.

interview.q: Where do the production files go after build?
interview.a: Into the dist/ folder, which you can upload to any static host.

topics.title: JSX: Syntax and Rules
topics.summary: JSX looks like HTML inside JavaScript but compiles to function calls and has stricter rules.
topics.description:
**JSX** is a syntax extension that lets you write markup inside JavaScript. A compiler (Babel or esbuild) turns `

Hello

` into a call like `jsx("h1", { children: "Hello" })` that returns a plain object called a React element. ### Rules you must remember - **One root element.** Return a single parent, or wrap in a **Fragment** `<>...` to avoid an extra DOM node. - **Close every tag.** Void elements are self-closing: ``, ``, `
`. - **camelCase attributes.** `className` instead of `class`, `htmlFor` instead of `for`, `onClick`, `tabIndex`. - **Expressions in braces.** `{user.name}`, `{a + b}`, `{items.length}`. Statements like `if` or `for` do not work inside braces. - **Style is an object.** `style={{ color: 'red', fontSize: 20 }}` - double braces are an object inside an expression. - **Comments** inside JSX use `{/* comment */}`. - **Booleans, null and undefined** render nothing. - JSX **escapes** values by default, which protects against XSS. ### Components start with a capital letter `

topics.title: Components and Props
topics.summary: Components are functions that return UI; props are the read-only inputs you pass to them.
topics.description:
A **component** is a JavaScript function that returns JSX. Components let you split the UI into independent pieces you can reuse and test. Modern React uses **function components**; class components still exist but are rarely written for new code. ### Props **Props** (properties) are the arguments to a component. You pass them like HTML attributes and read them from the first function parameter, usually with destructuring. ```jsx function Greeting({ name, age = 18 }) { return

{name} is {age}

; } ``` ### Rules - Props are **read-only**. A component must never modify its own props (it is a pure function of props and state). - Pass strings in quotes, anything else in braces: `age={20}`, `active={true}`, `items={list}`. - Use **default values** in destructuring: `{ size = "md" }`. - Use the spread syntax to forward many props: ``. - Pass **functions** as props to let children talk to parents (events go up). ### Naming and file layout Component names are PascalCase. One component per file is a good habit, with the file named after the component.

Non-string props need braces: count={5}

Forgetting braces: count="5" passes a string, not a number.

interview.a: No. Props are read-only. If a component needs to change data, it should use state or ask the parent through a callback prop.

interview.q: How do you set default prop values?
interview.a: Use default values in destructuring, like function Button({ size = "md" }). The old defaultProps on function components is deprecated.

topics.title: Conditional Rendering
topics.summary: Show different UI based on state or props using if, ternary, && and early returns.
topics.description:
In React, conditional rendering is just JavaScript. You choose what JSX to return using normal expressions.

### Techniques

- **`if` with early return** - best for loading/error/empty states.
- **Ternary** `cond ? <A /> : <B />` - choose between two outputs inline.
- **Logical AND** `cond && <A />` - render something or nothing.
- **Variable assignment** - compute `let content;` using `if` / `switch`, then render `{content}`.
- **Returning `null`** - render nothing from a component.
- **Lookup object** - `const views = { a: <A/>, b: <B/> }; views[status]`.

### The `0` gotcha

`count && <List />` renders the number `0` when `count` is `0`, because React renders numbers. Convert to boolean: `count > 0 && <List />`.

### Hiding vs removing

Returning `null` *unmounts* the component and discards its state. If you want to keep state while hiding, use CSS (`display: none` or the `hidden` attribute).

### Keep it readable

Nested ternaries get ugly. Extract small components or use early returns instead.

cond && <X/> renders nothing for false/null/undefined
Ternary picks between two branches inline
null return unmounts and drops state
Beware 0 && <X/> rendering a literal 0
pitfalls: Using array.length && <List/> and seeing a stray 0 on screen.
Deeply nested ternaries; extract components instead.

interview.q: Why can `{count && <Foo/>}` show a 0?
interview.a: Because when count is 0 the && expression returns 0, and React renders numbers. Use count > 0 && ... or a ternary.

interview.q: Difference between returning null and hiding with CSS?
interview.a: Returning null unmounts the component and loses its state; CSS hiding keeps it mounted with state intact.

To render a list, use `Array.prototype.map` to turn data into JSX elements. Each element in the list needs a **`key`** prop. ```jsx

    • )}
``` ### What keys do Keys tell React which item is which between renders. With stable keys React can reorder, insert and remove items correctly and keep each item's state (for example text typed in an input) attached to the right item. ### Choosing a key - Best: a **stable unique id** from your data (database id, UUID). - OK: an index, **only** if the list is static and never reordered, filtered or edited. - Never: `Math.random()` or `Date.now()` during render - the key changes every time so React recreates every item. ### Rules - Keys must be unique **among siblings**, not globally. - The `key` is not passed as a prop; read it separately if needed. - Put the key on the outermost element returned from `map`, e.g. on `` when needed. ### Filtering and sorting Do `filter`/`sort` before `map`. topics.title: Handling Events
topics.summary: Attach event handlers with camelCase props and pass functions, not function calls.
topics.description:
React wraps browser events in a **SyntheticEvent** that behaves the same across browsers. You attach handlers using camelCase props: `onClick`, `onChange`, `onSubmit`, `onKeyDown`, `onMouseEnter` and so on.

### Pass a function, do not call it

```jsx
<button onClick={handleClick}>OK</button>       // correct
<button onClick={() => remove(id)}>Delete</button> // pass args
<button onClick={handleClick()}>Bad</button>    // runs during render!
```

### The event object

Handlers receive an event: `e.target` (element that triggered it), `e.currentTarget` (element the handler is on), `e.preventDefault()` (stop default behavior such as form submit), `e.stopPropagation()` (stop bubbling).

### Common handlers

| Event | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `onClick` | buttons, links |
| `onChange` | inputs, selects (fires on every keystroke) |
| `onSubmit` | forms; call `e.preventDefault()` |
| `onKeyDown` | keyboard shortcuts, Enter to submit |

### Notes

- Handler names: write `handleX` for the function, `onX` for the prop.
- Events bubble; React attaches listeners at the root container.
- Since React 17 there is no event pooling; you can read `e` asynchronously.
- Capture phase is available with `onClickCapture`.

Pass the function reference, not its call result
Use arrow functions to pass arguments
e.preventDefault() stops form submit / link navigation
Events bubble; e.stopPropagation() stops them
pitfalls: onClick={doThing()} calls the function while rendering.
Forgetting e.preventDefault() in onSubmit, which reloads the page.

interview.q: What is a SyntheticEvent?
interview.a: A cross-browser wrapper around the native event with the same interface (target, preventDefault, stopPropagation, etc.).

interview.q: Why does onClick={fn()} run immediately?
interview.a: Because fn() is evaluated during render and its return value is what gets passed. Pass fn or () => fn() instead.

topics.title: Component Composition and Thinking in React
topics.summary: Break a UI into a tree of small components and decide where each piece of state lives.
topics.description:
Building React apps is mostly about **composition**: assembling small components into bigger ones. The official "Thinking in React" process has five steps.

### The 5 steps

1. **Break the UI into a component hierarchy.** Draw boxes around each piece. A component should ideally do one thing (single responsibility).
2. **Build a static version** using props only - no state yet.
3. **Find the minimal state.** Keep only what changes and cannot be calculated from other data.
4. **Decide where state lives.** Put it in the closest common parent of all components that need it.
5. **Add inverse data flow.** Pass callbacks down so children can update parent state.

### Composition patterns

- **Containment** - use `children` for generic boxes.
- **Specialization** - a `ConfirmDialog` renders a generic `Dialog` with specific props.
- **Slots** - pass JSX via props like `header` or `icon`.

### Why not inheritance?

React recommends composition for code reuse. You almost never need class inheritance between components.

### Rules of thumb

- If a component file grows beyond ~150 lines or does several jobs, split it.
- Data flows one way: parent to child.
- Avoid duplicating state; derive values during render.

Build static first (props), then add state
Keep minimal state; derive everything else
State lives in the closest common parent
Use children, props and slots for reuse, not inheritance
pitfalls: Putting all UI in one giant component.
Storing derived values in state, which later goes out of sync.

interview.q: What are the steps of Thinking in React?
interview.a: Split the UI into components, build a static version, identify minimal state, decide where state lives, and add inverse data flow with callbacks.

interview.q: Why does React favor composition over inheritance?
interview.a: Composition via props and children is more flexible and explicit; inheritance couples components tightly and is rarely needed.

topics.title: useState: Adding State
topics.summary: useState gives a component memory; calling its setter re-renders with the new value.
topics.description:
Normal local variables reset on every render and changing them does not update the screen. **State** solves both problems: it is remembered between renders and changing it tells React to render again.

```jsx
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
```

`useState(initial)` returns an array of two items: the **current value** and a **setter function**. Array destructuring lets you name them freely (`[value, setValue]`).

### How it behaves

- The initial value is used only on the **first** render.
- Calling `setCount(5)` schedules a re-render. The new value is available in the **next** render, not on the next line.
- If the new value is identical (`Object.is`) to the old one, React skips the re-render.
- Each component instance has its **own** state. Two `<Counter />` elements do not share a count.
- State is tied to the component's position in the tree. If the component unmounts, state is lost.

### Lazy initial state

If computing the initial value is expensive, pass a function: `useState(() => readFromStorage())`. React calls it only once.

### What belongs in state?

Only values that change over time **and** affect what is rendered. Values you can compute from other state or props should not be state. Values that change but do not affect the UI (timer ids, previous values) belong in a `ref`.

interview.a: A normal variable resets every render and does not trigger a re-render. State persists and updating it re-renders the component.

interview.q: Why does console.log(count) right after setCount show the old value?
interview.a: State is a snapshot for that render. The setter only schedules a new render in which count will have the new value.

topics.title: Functional Updates and Batching
topics.summary: Use the updater form when the next state depends on the previous one; React batches multiple updates into one render.
topics.description:
Inside one render, `count` is a fixed **snapshot**. So this does not add 3:

```jsx
setCount(count + 1);
setCount(count + 1);
setCount(count + 1); // count is 0 in all three -> result 1
```

### Functional (updater) form

Pass a function that receives the latest pending state:

```jsx
setCount(c => c + 1);
setCount(c => c + 1);
setCount(c => c + 1); // result 3
```

Use this form whenever the new value is calculated **from the previous value**, especially in effects, timers and async callbacks, where the closure may hold a stale value.

### Batching

React groups multiple state updates inside the same event into **one re-render**. Since React 18 this is **automatic batching** everywhere: event handlers, timeouts, promises and native events. You can rely on fewer renders without any extra code.

### Updater rules

- The updater function must be **pure** (no side effects, no mutation). In development React may call it twice.
- If you pass a value that depends on nothing else (`setName("Asha")`), the plain form is fine.
- To force a synchronous DOM update (rare) you can use `flushSync` from `react-dom`.

Use setX(prev => next) when depending on previous state
React batches updates into a single render (automatic batching in 18+)
Updater functions must be pure

Using stale state inside setInterval callbacks; use the updater form.

interview.a: React 18 groups multiple state updates, even inside promises, timeouts and native handlers, into one re-render.

topics.title: Updating Objects and Arrays Immutably
topics.summary: Never mutate state; create a new object or array so React can see the change.
topics.description:
React decides whether to re-render by comparing the old and new state with `Object.is`. If you mutate an object or array in place, the reference stays the same, so React sees "no change" and may skip the update. Therefore state must be treated as **read-only**: always make a copy.

### Objects

Use the spread operator and override the changed key:

```jsx
setUser({ ...user, age: user.age + 1 });
// nested
setUser({ ...user, address: { ...user.address, city: "Pune" } });
```

### Arrays

| Goal | Avoid (mutates) | Use (returns new) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| add | `push`, `unshift` | `[...arr, x]`, `[x, ...arr]` |

### Deep nesting

Deeply nested updates become verbose. Keep state **flat** where possible, or use a helper such as **Immer** (`use-immer`, or Redux Toolkit which includes it) so you can write "mutating" code that is applied immutably.

### Why immutability?

It makes change detection cheap, enables `memo`, time-travel debugging, and avoids hard-to-trace bugs where two parts of the app share the same object.

topics.title: Controlled Inputs and Forms
topics.summary: In a controlled input, React state is the single source of truth for the value.
topics.description:
A **controlled component** is a form element whose `value` is driven by state and whose changes are reported through `onChange`. The DOM never holds a value that React does not know about.

```jsx
const [name, setName] = useState("");
<input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />
```

### Why control inputs?

- Validate or format as the user types (uppercase, trim, limit).
- Disable submit until the form is valid.
- Reset or prefill the form by changing state.
- Show the current value elsewhere on the page.

### Different input types

| Element | Value prop | Read from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| text, textarea, select | `value` | `e.target.value` |
| checkbox | `checked` | `e.target.checked` |
| radio | `checked` | `e.target.value` |
| file | uncontrolled only | `e.target.files` |

### One handler for many fields

Give inputs a `name` and use a single handler with a computed key: `setForm({ ...form, [e.target.name]: e.target.value })`.

### Controlled vs uncontrolled

Uncontrolled inputs use `defaultValue` and read the value with a `ref` or `FormData` on submit. They are simpler and cause fewer re-renders. Controlled inputs are better when you need live validation. Never switch an input between the two (React warns).

topics.title: Lifting State Up
topics.summary: When two components need the same data, move the state to their closest common parent and pass it down.
topics.description:
Sometimes two sibling components must reflect the same changing data, for example a temperature in Celsius and Fahrenheit, or a filter input and a result list. Siblings cannot talk to each other directly. The solution is to **lift state up**: move it to their nearest common ancestor.

### The recipe

1. Remove the state from the children.
2. Declare the state in the parent.
3. Pass the value **down** as a prop.
4. Pass a **setter callback** down (an `onChange` prop) so children can request updates.

The children become **controlled components**: they display what the parent tells them and notify the parent on change.

### Single source of truth

Every piece of data should live in exactly one component. Other components receive it as props. If you find two states that must be kept equal with an effect, you almost certainly need to lift one.

### When lifting gets painful

If state is lifted very high and passed through many layers (**prop drilling**), consider Context, composition (passing JSX as `children`), or a state library. Do not use them preemptively; lift only as far as needed.

### Data flow

Props flow down, events flow up. This one-way flow makes it easy to find who owns a piece of data.

topics.title: Derived State and Choosing State
topics.summary: Compute values from existing state during render instead of storing duplicates.
topics.description:
**Derived state** is data you can calculate from other state or props. The rule: **do not store it in state; compute it during render.**

### Bad pattern

```jsx
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);   // duplicate!
useEffect(() => setCount(items.length), [items]);
```

This renders twice, can show a stale count for one frame, and forgets to sync in some code path.

### Good pattern

```jsx
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
const count = items.length;
const done = items.filter(i => i.done).length;
```

### Principles for structuring state

- **Group related state** that always changes together into one object or reducer.
- **Avoid contradictions**: use `status: "idle" | "loading" | "error"` instead of `isLoading` and `isError` booleans that can both be true.
- **Avoid redundant state**: if you can calculate it, calculate it.
- **Avoid duplication**: store a selected item's `id`, not a copy of the whole object, so edits stay in sync.
- **Avoid deeply nested state**: flatten it.

### Expensive calculations

If a derivation is slow, wrap it in `useMemo`. Measure first; most derivations are cheap.

### Copying props into state

`useState(props.value)` only uses the prop on the first render. If the prop should keep driving the UI, do not copy it. Use a `key` to reset state when identity changes.

topics.title: useEffect: Running Side Effects
topics.summary: useEffect runs code after render to sync your component with something outside React.
topics.description:
A **side effect** is anything that reaches outside the component's pure render calculation: fetching data, setting up a subscription, changing `document.title`, starting a timer, or touching a non-React widget. `useEffect` runs such code **after** React has painted the screen.

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  document.title = `Count: ${count}`;
}, [count]);
```

### The dependency array

| Form | When the effect runs |
| --- | --- |
| `useEffect(fn)` | after **every** render |
| `useEffect(fn, [])` | once after mount (and cleanup on unmount) |
| `useEffect(fn, [a, b])` | after mount and whenever `a` or `b` changed |

React compares dependencies with `Object.is`. **Every reactive value used inside the effect** (props, state, functions defined in the component) must be listed. The `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` ESLint rule enforces this.

### Think in synchronization

Do not think "run on mount / update". Think: "While these values are what they are, keep this outside thing in sync with them". When a dependency changes, React cleans up the old effect and re-synchronizes.

### You might not need an effect

Do not use effects for: transforming data for render (compute it), responding to user events (use the handler), or resetting state when a prop changes (use `key`). Effects are for syncing with external systems.

topics.title: Effect Cleanup
topics.summary: Return a cleanup function to undo what the effect set up: timers, listeners, subscriptions.
topics.description:
An effect can return a function. React calls it **before the effect runs again** and **when the component unmounts**. This is where you undo the setup so nothing leaks.

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(tick, 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, []);
```

### Typical cleanups

- `clearInterval` / `clearTimeout`
- `removeEventListener`
- `socket.close()` / `unsubscribe()`
- `controller.abort()` for fetch
- Destroying third-party widgets (maps, charts)

### Order of events

On a dependency change: React runs the **old cleanup**, then the **new effect**. On unmount: only the cleanup. Cleanup closes over the values from the render that created the effect, so it always cleans up the right thing.

### Why it matters

Without cleanup you get duplicate listeners, memory leaks, and "state update on an unmounted component" bugs. In development with `StrictMode`, React deliberately runs setup, cleanup, setup on mount to expose missing cleanups.

### Writing symmetrical effects

Good effects are symmetrical: whatever setup does, cleanup undoes. If cleanup is hard to write, the effect may be doing too much or may belong in an event handler.

topics.title: StrictMode and Double Invocation
topics.summary: In development StrictMode runs renders and effects twice to expose impure code and missing cleanup.
topics.description:
`<StrictMode>` is a development-only wrapper that helps you find bugs early. It has **no effect on production builds**.

### What it does (React 18/19)

- **Re-renders components twice** to detect impure rendering. Your component should give the same output both times.
- **Runs effects twice on mount**: setup, cleanup, setup again. This simulates a component being unmounted and remounted, which React may do for features like Offscreen and fast refresh.
- **Re-runs ref callbacks** (React 19).
- Warns about deprecated APIs.

### Why does my effect run twice?

That is the most common question. It is not a bug in React. It is a test: if your effect, cleanup and re-setup leave the app in a correct state, your effect is resilient. If you see duplicated network calls, duplicated listeners or a doubled counter, it reveals a missing cleanup.

### How to fix real problems

- Add proper **cleanup** (abort fetch, remove listener, close socket).
- Keep render **pure**: do not mutate variables outside the component, do not push to a global array in render.
- For one-time app initialization (not per component) put the code outside the component at module level.
- Do not "fix" it by removing StrictMode or using a `ref` flag to skip the second run; that hides the bug.

### Production

The double invocation never happens in the production build, so users see a single run.

topics.title: useRef: Mutable Values Without Re-rendering
topics.summary: useRef stores a mutable value that persists across renders and does not trigger a re-render when changed.
topics.description:
`useRef(initial)` returns a plain object `{ current: initial }` that React keeps the **same object** across renders. You can read and write `ref.current` freely. Unlike state, **changing a ref does not re-render** the component.

### When to use a ref

- Keep **timer ids** (`intervalRef.current = setInterval(...)`).
- Store **previous values** (`prevRef.current = value` in an effect).
- Count renders, track "is mounted", hold the latest callback.
- Keep any value that is **not needed for rendering output**.
- Hold **DOM nodes** (next topic).

### Ref vs state

| | State | Ref |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Re-render on change | yes | no |
| Persists across renders | yes | yes |
| Can be read during render | yes | avoid |
| Mutable directly | no | yes |

### Rules

- Do not read or write `ref.current` **during rendering** (except for lazy initialization), because it makes the component impure and unpredictable. Use it in event handlers and effects.
- If the screen should change when a value changes, it belongs in state.
- Refs are the "escape hatch" for stepping outside React's data flow; use them sparingly.

topics.title: Accessing the DOM with Refs

Sometimes you must talk to the DOM directly: focus an input, scroll to an element, play a video, measure a size or hook up a third-party library. Create a ref and pass it to the `ref` attribute of a JSX element.

```jsx
const inputRef = useRef(null);
```

- `focus()`, `select()`, `blur()`
- `scrollIntoView()`
- `video.play()` / `pause()`
- Measuring with `getBoundingClientRect()`
- Integrating charts, maps, editors

`ref={node => {...}}` is called with the node on mount and `null` on unmount. Useful for dynamic lists or measuring when a node appears. Since React 19 callback refs may return a cleanup function.

### Refs to components

Ref is a normal prop in React 19 function components. In React 18 you must wrap the child in `forwardRef` to expose a DOM node of the child.

### Do not overuse

Do not use refs to change what React manages (adding classes, setting text). Let state drive the DOM; use refs only for imperative actions that cannot be expressed as props.

topics.title: Rules of Hooks
topics.summary: Call hooks only at the top level of function components or custom hooks, in the same order every render.
topics.description:
Hooks are functions whose names start with `use`: `useState`, `useEffect`, `useContext` and so on. React identifies each hook by its **call order** in the component, not by name. That is why there are two strict rules.

### The two rules

1. **Only call hooks at the top level.** Not inside `if`, loops, nested functions, `try/catch` blocks, or after an early `return`.
2. **Only call hooks from React functions.** Function components or other custom hooks (functions starting with `use`). Never from regular JS functions or class components.

### Why order matters

React stores hook state in a linked list attached to the component. On every render it walks the list in order. If one render skips a hook, all following hooks read the wrong slot and state gets mixed up.

### Fixing conditional hooks

```jsx
// Wrong
if (user) { const [x, setX] = useState(0); }

// Right: call hook always, condition inside
const [x, setX] = useState(0);
if (!user) return null;
```

Put early returns **after** all hooks, or move the conditional part into its own child component.

### Tooling

Install `eslint-plugin-react-hooks`. It enforces `rules-of-hooks` and `exhaustive-deps`. Vite templates include it. In React 19 the new `use` API is the exception: it can be called conditionally.

topics.title: Context API and useContext
topics.summary: Context lets you share values with deeply nested components without passing props through every level.
topics.description:
**Context** solves *prop drilling*. A provider component makes a value available to everything below it, and any descendant can read it with `useContext`, no matter how deep.

### Three steps

1. **Create** the context: `const ThemeContext = createContext("light");` (the argument is the default value used when there is no provider).
2. **Provide** a value: `<ThemeContext.Provider value={theme}>...</ThemeContext.Provider>`. In React 19 you can write `<ThemeContext value={theme}>`.
3. **Consume**: `const theme = useContext(ThemeContext);`

### How updates work

When the provider's `value` changes (compared by reference), **every component that calls `useContext` for that context re-renders**, even if `memo` wraps it. Parents between the provider and consumers are not forced to re-render.

### Good use cases

Theme, current user, locale, router information, feature flags, toast/notification API. Data that is read by many components at different depths and changes infrequently.

### Limits

- Context is not a full state manager. It has no selectors: any change re-renders all consumers.
- An object literal as value (`value={{ user, setUser }}`) creates a new reference each render. Memoize it with `useMemo` if the provider re-renders often.
- Put providers as low in the tree as practical.

topics.title: useMemo: Caching Calculations
topics.summary: useMemo remembers the result of an expensive calculation until its dependencies change.
topics.description:
`useMemo(calculate, dependencies)` runs `calculate` during render, caches the returned value, and returns the cached value on later renders unless a dependency changed.

```jsx
const visible = useMemo(() => filterTodos(todos, filter), [todos, filter]);
```

### Typical uses

1. **Skipping an expensive calculation** (sorting or filtering thousands of items). Measure first; `console.time` a calculation of ~1ms or more is worth it.
2. **Keeping a stable reference** (object or array) so that a child wrapped in `memo`, or another hook's dependency array, does not see a "new" value every render.
3. **Memoizing context values.**

### What it is not

- It is a **performance hint, not a semantic guarantee**. React may discard the cache (for example for offscreen content), so your code must still work without it.
- It does not reduce the first-render cost.
- Memoizing everything adds comparison overhead and code noise. Most calculations are cheap.

### Rules

- The function must be pure.
- Include all reactive values used inside in the dependency array.
- Do not use it to run side effects (use `useEffect`).
- With the React Compiler (see performance section) most manual memoization becomes unnecessary.

topics.title: useCallback: Stable Function References
topics.summary: useCallback returns the same function instance between renders until dependencies change.
topics.description:
Every render creates **new function objects**. Usually that is harmless. It matters only when the function identity is compared: passed to a `memo`-wrapped child, or listed in the dependency array of `useEffect`, `useMemo`, etc.

```jsx
const handleSave = useCallback((id) => {
  save(id);
}, [save]);
```

`useCallback(fn, deps)` is the same as `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`.

### When it actually helps

1. Passing a callback to a child wrapped in `React.memo` - without a stable function the memo is useless.
2. A function used as a dependency of `useEffect` where re-running on every render would be wrong.
3. A function stored in a custom hook returned to consumers who will use it in dependencies.

### When it does not help

- Passing handlers to plain DOM elements (`<button onClick=...>`).
- Passing to children that are **not** memoized (they re-render anyway).
- Tiny components where re-render is cheap.

### Avoiding stale state

Use the **functional updater** to avoid depending on state: `setItems(prev => [...prev, x])` lets you keep `[]` as dependencies.

### Alternatives

topics.title: React.memo: Skipping Re-renders
topics.summary: memo wraps a component so it re-renders only when its props change (shallow comparison).
topics.description:
By default, when a parent re-renders, **all of its children re-render**, even if their props did not change. `React.memo` wraps a component and tells React: "skip re-rendering this one if the new props are shallowly equal to the old props".

```jsx
const Row = memo(function Row({ item, onSelect }) { ... });
```

### Shallow comparison

React compares each prop with `Object.is`. Primitives (numbers, strings, booleans) compare by value. Objects, arrays and functions compare by **reference**, so a new `{}` or `() => {}` created in the parent on each render defeats `memo`.

### Making memo effective

- Pass primitives where possible.
- Stabilize objects with `useMemo` and functions with `useCallback`.
- Pass `children` carefully - JSX children are a new object each render.
- Provide a custom comparison function as 2nd argument only if truly necessary (it is easy to get wrong).

### When to use memo

- A component is **expensive** to render (big list rows, charts).
- It re-renders **often** with the **same props**.
- You have *measured* a problem with the Profiler.

### When not to

Most components are cheap. Memoizing adds comparison cost and complexity. Do not wrap everything.

### Notes

- State inside the memoized component still triggers its own re-render.
- Context changes bypass memo.
- The React Compiler can automate memoization.

Parents re-rendering normally re-renders all children
New object/function props break memo

Use after profiling, not by default

Writing a custom comparator that ignores props which later change.

interview.a: It memoizes a component so it only re-renders if its props changed according to a shallow comparison.

interview.a: A new object literal is created on each parent render, so its reference differs and the shallow comparison fails. Memoize it with useMemo.

topics.title: useLayoutEffect vs useEffect
topics.summary: useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM updates but before the browser paints; use it for measuring and preventing flicker.
topics.description:
Both hooks run after React updates the DOM, but at different moments:

| | `useEffect` | `useLayoutEffect` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timing | after the browser **paints** | after DOM update, **before paint** |
| Blocks painting | no | yes |
| Typical use | fetching, subscriptions, logging | measuring DOM, positioning |

### When you need useLayoutEffect

When you must **read layout** (size, position via `getBoundingClientRect`) and **synchronously update state** based on it, so the user never sees the intermediate wrong frame. Examples: tooltips and popovers placed next to a target, auto-growing textareas, scroll position restoration, animations that start from measured values.

```jsx
useLayoutEffect(() => {
  const { height } = ref.current.getBoundingClientRect();
  setHeight(height);
}, []);
```

### Cautions

- It **blocks the browser from painting**, so slow code here makes the UI feel janky. Keep it tiny.
- It does not run on the server (`renderToString`); React warns. Use `useEffect` or `useIsomorphicLayoutEffect` for SSR code.
- Default to `useEffect`. Switch only if you see a flicker.
- The setState inside triggers a synchronous re-render before paint.

Use to measure layout and avoid visual flicker
Blocks paint, so keep it fast
Not run on the server; warns in SSR
Default to useEffect

interview.a: Layout effects cannot run during server rendering, so React warns; use useEffect or an isomorphic wrapper.

topics.title: useId: Stable Unique IDs
topics.summary: useId generates a unique id that is the same on server and client, for linking labels and inputs.
topics.description:
Accessibility needs ids: `<label htmlFor="email">` points to `<input id="email">`. Hard-coding ids breaks when the component is rendered more than once (two forms on a page share the same id). `useId()` solves both. It returns a string like `:r1:` that is **stable across server and client** and **unique per call site**.

```jsx
function Field({ label }) {
  const id = useId();
  return (
    <>
      <label htmlFor={id}>{label}</label>
      <input id={id} />
    </>
  );
}
```

Need several ids in one component? Call `useId()` once and add suffixes: `${id}-error`, `${id}-hint`. Great for `aria-describedby`.

### What NOT to do

- **Do not use it for list keys.** Keys should come from your data.
- Do not use it for CSS selectors (the colon characters need escaping).
- Do not call it conditionally (it is a hook).

### Why useful

It makes reusable form components safe: render `<Field />` ten times and every label correctly points to its own input.

topics.title: useTransition: Non-blocking Updates
topics.summary: useTransition marks a state update as low priority so the UI stays responsive during heavy re-renders.
topics.description:
Some updates are urgent (typing, clicking) and some can wait (filtering a huge list, switching a heavy tab). **Transitions** let you mark the second kind as non-urgent so React can interrupt them if something more urgent happens.

```jsx
const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

function onChange(e) {
  setQuery(e.target.value);                 // urgent: update input
  startTransition(() => setFilter(e.target.value)); // can wait
}
```

### What you get

- `startTransition(fn)` - state updates inside `fn` are low priority. React renders them in the background and discards them if new input arrives.
- `isPending` - `true` while the transition is rendering, to show a subtle spinner or dim the list.

### How it keeps the UI smooth

Without a transition, a slow render blocks the main thread and typing feels laggy. With it, React renders the heavy part in small chunks and yields to the browser.

### Rules

- Only works for **state updates** (not for controlling inputs' own value; the input should update urgently).
- The function passed must run **synchronously** (in React 18; React 19 supports async functions as "Actions").
- Transitions keep the **old UI** visible while new content is rendering, and with Suspense avoid replacing it with a fallback.
- There is a standalone `startTransition` import when you do not need `isPending`.

Input value must still update urgently
Works well with Suspense and heavy lists

topics.title: useDeferredValue
topics.summary: useDeferredValue gives you a lagging copy of a value so expensive UI can catch up without blocking typing.
topics.description:
`useDeferredValue(value)` returns the same value on the first render, and on updates it first returns the **old value** while React re-renders in the background with the **new value**. Once the background render finishes, the deferred value catches up.

```jsx

const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query);
// input uses query, slow list uses deferredQuery
<SlowList filter={deferredQuery} />
```

### Compared to useTransition

- `useTransition` wraps the **setter** (you control the update).
- `useDeferredValue` wraps the **value** (you receive it as a prop and cannot touch the setter), which is ideal inside child components or with props from libraries.

### Making it effective

Wrap the slow child in `memo`. Otherwise the child re-renders anyway with the urgent render. Pass the deferred value only to the slow part.

### Showing stale state

`query !== deferredQuery` tells you the UI is behind, so you can dim the list.

### Not debouncing

Debounce waits a fixed time, then runs. `useDeferredValue` has no fixed delay: it adapts to the device (a fast computer catches up immediately) and the background render is interruptible. It does **not** reduce network requests, so still debounce API calls.

topics.title: useSyncExternalStore
topics.summary: Subscribe safely to any external store (browser APIs, Redux-like stores) with tear-free updates.
topics.description:
Not all data lives in React state. Browser APIs (`navigator.onLine`, `matchMedia`), third-party stores (Redux, Zustand internally) and your own global objects change outside React. `useSyncExternalStore` is the official way to read them and re-render when they change.

```jsx
const value = useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot);
```

### The three arguments

- **`subscribe(callback)`** - registers `callback` to be called when the store changes and returns an **unsubscribe** function.
- **`getSnapshot()`** - returns the current value. It must return the **same reference** if nothing changed (otherwise React loops forever). Never create a new object each call.
- **`getServerSnapshot()`** - value used during server rendering and hydration (optional on client-only apps).

### Why not useEffect + useState?

In concurrent rendering, a store may change while React is rendering in slices, giving parts of the UI different values (**tearing**). `useSyncExternalStore` forces a consistent, synchronous read, so there is no tearing.

### Where you see it

State libraries use it internally. In your own code it is great for `useOnlineStatus`, `useMediaQuery`, `useWindowWidth`, and a tiny global store.

### Tips

Define `subscribe` outside the component or memoize it; otherwise it resubscribes every render.

topics.title: Composition vs Inheritance
topics.summary: React favors building components by combining them (props, children, slots) rather than extending classes.
topics.description:
In classical OOP, you might reuse code by creating `class SpecialButton extends Button`. React's recommendation is the opposite: **use composition**. Facebook has thousands of components and found no case that required component inheritance.

### Composition tools

1. **Containment** - a generic component renders `props.children`: `Card`, `Modal`, `Layout`.
2. **Specialization** - a "specific" component renders a "generic" one with preset props: `<DangerButton>` renders `<Button variant="danger" />`.
3. **Slots** - pass JSX through named props: `<Layout sidebar={<Nav />} content={<Feed />} />`.
4. **Custom hooks** - share logic (not UI).
5. **Context** - share data without drilling.

### Why composition wins

- **Explicit data flow:** you see which props go in.
- **Flexible:** change markup at the call site without editing the library component.
- **No fragile base-class problem:** changing a base class cannot silently break children.
- **Easy to test.**

### Anti-pattern: boolean prop explosion

`<Button primary large rounded outline icon loading />` grows endlessly. Prefer variants (`variant="primary"`) or composition (`<Button><Icon/> Save</Button>`).

### Sharing non-UI logic

If you want to reuse a function, import it. If you want to reuse stateful logic, write a custom hook. Neither needs inheritance.

```jsx
  <Tabs.Panel value="b">Second</Tabs.Panel>
```

The parent (`Tabs`) holds the state and shares it with its sub-components through **Context**. Children read state from context, so the user does not pass props manually and the layout can be reordered or wrapped freely.

- **Flexible markup** - the consumer controls structure and order.
- **Clean API** - fewer props, no config arrays.
- **Encapsulated state** - the internal logic is hidden.
- Used by Radix UI, Headless UI, Reach UI, Chakra, MUI.

### Implementation tips

- Use `createContext` and a custom hook that throws when used outside the parent.
- Attach children as static properties: `Tabs.Tab = Tab`.
- Make accessibility part of the pattern: ARIA roles and keyboard handling.
- Support controlled mode (`value` + `onValueChange`) and uncontrolled (`defaultValue`).

topics.title: Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components
topics.summary: Controlled components get their value from props/state; uncontrolled ones keep it internally in the DOM or their own state.
topics.description:
This concept applies to inputs **and** to any reusable component with a value (toggle, tabs, accordion, modal open state).

### Controlled

The parent owns the state and passes `value` plus `onChange`. The component is a pure view of props.

- Single source of truth in React.
- Easy validation, formatting, syncing and resetting.
- More code and re-renders.

### Uncontrolled

The component (or the DOM) holds its own state. You set an initial value with `defaultValue` / `defaultOpen` and read the result with a ref, `FormData`, or an `onChange` notification.

- Less code, fewer renders.
- Harder to reset or validate live.

### Supporting both in your own component

Good library components (Radix, MUI) accept both: if the `value` prop is given they are controlled, otherwise they manage internal state.

```jsx
function useControllable(value, defaultValue, onChange) {
  const [inner, setInner] = useState(defaultValue);
  const controlled = value !== undefined;
  const current = controlled ? value : inner;
  const set = (v) => { if (!controlled) setInner(v); onChange?.(v); };
  return [current, set];
}
```

### Choosing

Use **uncontrolled** with `FormData` for simple submit-only forms. Use **controlled** when the UI reacts to the value while typing or when other components depend on it.

### Never mix

Switching between the two for the same element (value going from `undefined` to a string) triggers a warning and bugs.

topics.title: Container and Presentational Components
topics.summary: Separate components that know how things look from components that know how data is loaded and managed.
topics.description:
A classic way to organize components:

- **Presentational components** care about *how things look*. They receive data and callbacks via props, rarely have state (only UI state), and are easy to reuse and test (or document in Storybook).
- **Container components** care about *how things work*: fetching, state, calling APIs, connecting to Redux. They render presentational components and pass data down.

### Example

`UserList` (presentational) renders `users` it is given. `UserListContainer` fetches the users and passes them in.

### Modern take

Dan Abramov, who popularized the idea, later said you do not have to follow it strictly. **Hooks** let you separate logic without separate container components: put the logic in a custom hook (`useUsers`) and call it in the same component or a thin parent. The *principle* remains useful: keep rendering code free of data-fetching details.

### Benefits

- **Reusability** - the same view with different data sources.
- **Testing** - test the view with plain props, mock the hook separately.
- **Design system friendly** - dumb components can live in a UI library.
- **Cleaner components** - less mixing of concerns.

### Guidelines

- Presentational components should not import API clients or stores.
- Pass data as props; pass actions as callbacks.
- Do not split just for the sake of it; a tiny component that fetches and renders is fine.

topics.title: Portals
topics.summary: createPortal renders children into a different DOM node while keeping them in the same React tree.
topics.description:
Sometimes a component must visually escape its parent: modals, tooltips, dropdowns, toasts. If the parent has `overflow: hidden`, `transform` or a low `z-index`, a child cannot overlay everything. **Portals** render children into another DOM node, typically `document.body`. ```jsx import { createPortal } from "react-dom"; function Modal({ children }) { return createPortal(
{children}
, document.body); } ``` ### Key behaviors - **Events bubble through the React tree**, not the DOM tree. A click inside a portal still bubbles to React parents (useful, but surprising). - **Context works** through portals - they are still children of the provider. - State and lifecycle are the same as any child. - Only the physical DOM location changes. ### Typical use: accessible modal 1. Render into `document.body` via portal. 2. Add `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`. 3. Move focus into the dialog and **trap focus**; restore focus on close. 4. Close on **Escape** and overlay click. 5. Lock body scroll. The native `` element with `showModal()` also solves much of this, and is rendered in the top layer without a portal. ### Notes In a runnable preview, `document.body` is fine. In SSR, wait until mounted before using `document`.

topics.title: Error Boundaries
topics.summary: Catch rendering errors in a subtree and show a fallback UI instead of a blank screen.
topics.description:
If a component throws an error while rendering, React unmounts the **entire tree** by default, leaving a white screen. An **error boundary** catches errors from its children and renders a fallback.

### What they catch

- Errors during **rendering**
- Errors in **lifecycle methods**
- Errors in **constructors** of children

### What they do NOT catch

- Errors in **event handlers** (use try/catch)
- **Async** code (setTimeout, promises, fetch)
- **Server-side rendering** errors
- Errors thrown in the boundary itself

### Class component required

There is still no hook for it. A boundary uses `static getDerivedStateFromError(error)` to switch to a fallback and `componentDidCatch(error, info)` to log. Most teams use the **`react-error-boundary`** library, which gives `ErrorBoundary`, `fallbackRender`, `resetKeys` and `useErrorBoundary` (to forward async errors).

### Where to place them

- One around the whole app (last resort).
- Around risky or independent widgets (charts, comments) so a failure does not take the page down.
- Around each route.

### Recovery

Offer a "Try again" button that resets the boundary state, or use `resetKeys` so it resets when props change.

### Logging

Send errors and component stacks to Sentry or similar from `componentDidCatch`.

topics.title: Form Validation by Hand
topics.summary: Validate on blur and submit, keep errors in state, and show messages next to the fields.
topics.description:
Before reaching for a library, understand the manual approach. A validation flow has four parts.

### 1. Values and errors in state

Keep `values` (what the user typed), `errors` (messages by field name) and `touched` (fields the user has left) in state.

### 2. A pure `validate(values)` function

It returns an object like `{ email: "Invalid email" }`. Pure functions are easy to unit test and reuse on server and client.

### 3. When to validate

- **On submit** - always block the submit if there are errors.
- **On blur** - show an error when the user leaves a field (use `touched`) so you do not shout while they are still typing.
- **On change** - for fields that have been touched or already show an error, to clear the message as soon as it is fixed.

### 4. Accessible feedback

Link each error to its input with `aria-describedby`, set `aria-invalid`, move focus to the first invalid field on failed submit, and use `role="alert"` for dynamic messages.

### Client vs server validation

Client validation is for UX. **Never trust it for security**: the server must validate again, and it can return field errors that you map into the same `errors` state.

### When it gets heavy

Many fields, arrays, async checks and dependent fields quickly become repetitive. That is when React Hook Form and a schema library like Zod are worth it.

interview.a: After the user has interacted with the field (blur/touched) or tried to submit, not while they have not started typing.

interview.a: Users can bypass the browser, so the server must validate again for security and data integrity.

topics.title: React Hook Form
topics.summary: React Hook Form manages forms with minimal re-renders using uncontrolled inputs and a simple register API.
topics.description:
**React Hook Form (RHF)** is the most popular form library. It mostly uses **uncontrolled inputs** and refs under the hood, so typing in one field does not re-render the whole form. It also gives validation, error state, dirty/touched tracking and easy integration with schema validators.

### Core API

| API | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `useForm()` | creates the form instance |
| `register("name", rules)` | connects an input; returns `ref`, `name`, `onChange`, `onBlur` |
| `handleSubmit(fn)` | validates, then calls `fn(data)` |
| `formState.errors` | validation errors per field |
| `formState.isSubmitting`, `isDirty`, `isValid` | status flags |
| `watch("field")` | subscribe to value changes (causes re-render) |
| `reset()`, `setValue()`, `getValues()` | imperative control |
| `Controller` / `useController` | integrate controlled UI libs (MUI, Select) |
| `useFieldArray` | dynamic lists of inputs |

### Rules

Built-in rules: `required`, `min`, `max`, `minLength`, `maxLength`, `pattern`, `validate` (custom function, can be async).

### Why teams like it

- Very small bundle, no dependencies.
- Few re-renders - great for big forms.
- Works with TypeScript (typed form values).
- Pairs with `@hookform/resolvers` for Zod/Yup.

### Modes

`mode: "onSubmit"` (default), `"onBlur"`, `"onChange"`, `"onTouched"` decide when validation runs.

### Tips

Provide `defaultValues` for every field, use `Controller` for non-native inputs, and prefer `watch` sparingly.

topics.title: Schema Validation with Zod
topics.summary: Describe your data shape once with Zod, and reuse it for validation and TypeScript types.
topics.description:
**Zod** is a TypeScript-first schema library. You define a schema describing valid data, then parse input with it. The same schema gives you runtime validation **and** a static TypeScript type via `z.infer`.

```js
import { z } from "zod";

const signUpSchema = z.object({
  email: z.string().email("Invalid email"),
  password: z.string().min(8, "Min 8 chars"),
  confirm: z.string(),
  age: z.coerce.number().int().min(18, "Must be 18+"),
}).refine(d => d.password === d.confirm, {
  message: "Passwords do not match",
  path: ["confirm"],
});
```

### Parsing

- `schema.parse(data)` returns typed data or throws `ZodError`.
- `schema.safeParse(data)` returns `{ success, data | error }` without throwing.
- `error.flatten().fieldErrors` gives messages per field.

### Common building blocks

`z.string()`, `z.number()`, `z.boolean()`, `z.date()`, `z.enum([...])`, `z.array()`, `z.object()`, `.optional()`, `.nullable()`, `.default()`, `.transform()`, `.refine()`, `z.coerce.number()` (form values are strings!), `z.infer<typeof schema>`.

### With React Hook Form

Install `@hookform/resolvers` and pass `resolver: zodResolver(schema)` to `useForm`. Errors then flow into `formState.errors` automatically.

### Share between client and server

Put the schema in a shared package. The API validates incoming bodies with the very same schema, so rules never drift. Alternatives: Yup, Valibot, ArkType.

topics.title: File Upload and Preview
topics.summary: Read the selected file from an input, validate its type and size, preview it, and send it with FormData.
topics.description:
A file input is always **uncontrolled** in React; you cannot set its value. You read the selected files from `e.target.files` (a `FileList`) in the `onChange` handler.

### Steps

1. Render `<input type="file" accept="image/*" />` (add `multiple` for many files).
2. In `onChange`, take `e.target.files[0]`.
3. **Validate** `file.type` and `file.size` on the client (limits are for UX; the server must check again).
4. **Preview** images with `URL.createObjectURL(file)` and **revoke** the URL when done (cleanup) to avoid memory leaks. Alternatively use `FileReader.readAsDataURL`.
5. **Upload** with `FormData`:

```js
const fd = new FormData();
fd.append("avatar", file);
await fetch("/api/upload", { method: "POST", body: fd });
```

Do **not** set the `Content-Type` header yourself; the browser adds the multipart boundary.

### Progress

`fetch` has no upload progress. Use `XMLHttpRequest` (`xhr.upload.onprogress`) or axios `onUploadProgress`.

### Large files and production

Use **pre-signed URLs** (S3/GCS) so the browser uploads directly to storage, chunked/resumable uploads (tus), and drag-and-drop zones (`react-dropzone`). Always scan and validate on the server; never trust the file extension or MIME type sent by the client.

interview.a: createObjectURL keeps the file in memory until it is revoked, so cleaning up avoids memory leaks.

topics.title: Accessibility (a11y) in React
topics.summary: Use semantic HTML, labels, keyboard support, focus management and ARIA so everyone can use your app.
topics.description:
Accessibility means people using screen readers, keyboards, voice control or with low vision can use your UI. React renders ordinary HTML, so the same rules apply, with a few React-specific tools.

### The most important rules

1. **Semantic HTML first:** use `button`, `a`, `nav`, `main`, `ul`, `label`, headings in order. A clickable `<div>` has no keyboard support or role.
2. **Labels:** every input needs a `<label htmlFor>` (or `aria-label`). Use `useId` for unique ids.
3. **Keyboard:** everything clickable must be reachable with Tab and operable with Enter/Space. Never remove focus outlines without a replacement.
4. **Alt text:** meaningful `alt` for images; `alt=""` for decorative ones.
5. **Color contrast:** at least 4.5:1 for body text.
6. **Announce changes:** `role="alert"` or `aria-live="polite"` for toasts, errors and async results.

### React-specific tips

- Use **Fragments** to keep valid HTML structure (table rows, lists).
- `htmlFor`, `tabIndex`, `aria-*` and `role` are written as camelCase/lowercase attributes in JSX.
- **Manage focus** with refs when UI changes: move focus into a modal, back to the trigger on close, and to the new heading after a route change.
- Use `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y` to catch problems at build time.
- Test with the keyboard, a screen reader (NVDA, VoiceOver), axe DevTools and Lighthouse; `jest-axe` in unit tests.

### ARIA rule of thumb

*No ARIA is better than bad ARIA.* Use ARIA only when HTML cannot express the widget (tabs, combobox), and implement the full keyboard pattern.

topics.title: fetch vs axios in React
topics.summary: Both fetch and axios call APIs; axios adds interceptors, automatic JSON and error handling.
topics.description:
React has no built-in HTTP client. You use the browser's **`fetch`** or a library such as **axios**. Always call them from **effects, event handlers or data libraries**, never in the render body.

### fetch

```js
const res = await fetch("/api/users", { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } });
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
const users = await res.json();
```

- Built in, no dependency.
- Does **not reject on HTTP errors** (404/500) - check `res.ok`.
- You must call `res.json()` yourself and `JSON.stringify` request bodies and set `Content-Type`.
- Cancel with `AbortController`.

### axios

```js
const { data } = await axios.get("/api/users", { params: { page: 2 } });
```

- Rejects on non-2xx automatically; `error.response.status`, `error.response.data`.
- Auto JSON parse and stringify.
- **Instances** (`axios.create({ baseURL, timeout })`) and **interceptors** to attach tokens, refresh sessions or log errors in one place.
- Upload/download progress, cancellation via `signal`.

### Which to choose?

Use `fetch` for small apps (and wrap it in a tiny `api()` helper). Use axios if you want interceptors and tidy error handling. Both are fine; what matters more is using **TanStack Query/SWR** for caching and state.

### Good habits

- Keep API calls in a `services/` or `api/` folder, not scattered in components.
- Read the base URL from env variables.
- Never put secrets in front-end code.
- Handle loading, error and empty states.

topics.title: Loading, Error and Empty States
topics.summary: Every async screen has four states: loading, error, empty and success. Design all of them.
topics.description:
A request is never just "data or nothing". Real users see slow networks, failures and empty results. Handle all of these explicitly.

### The four states

| State | UI |
| --- | --- |
| **Loading** | skeleton or spinner (reserve layout to avoid jumping) |
| **Error** | friendly message + **Retry** button, log details |
| **Empty** | helpful text and a call to action ("No orders yet") |
| **Success** | the data |

### Modeling

Prefer a single `status` value (`"idle" | "loading" | "success" | "error"`) over separate booleans. It avoids impossible combinations and makes the render logic a simple switch.

### UX details

- Show **skeletons** rather than a spinner for content-heavy pages.
- Keep previous data visible while refetching (stale-while-revalidate) and show a subtle indicator.
- Use a **delay** (e.g. 200 ms) before showing a spinner to avoid flicker on fast requests.
- Distinguish **network error**, **404** and **500** when it helps.
- Do not hide forms or lose user input when a submit fails.
- Provide `aria-busy` and `role="alert"` for accessibility.

### Reuse

Create a small `<AsyncBoundary status error onRetry empty>` component or rely on TanStack Query's `isPending`, `isError`, `data` flags so each page does not reimplement this.

topics.title: Cancelling Requests with AbortController
topics.summary: Abort outdated requests when inputs change or components unmount to avoid wasted work and stale UI.
topics.description:
`AbortController` is a browser API that lets you cancel `fetch` (and many other APIs). It has a `signal` you pass to the request and an `abort()` method.

```js
const controller = new AbortController();
fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });
controller.abort();   // fetch rejects with name "AbortError"
```

### Why cancel in React

- **Search as you type:** earlier requests are useless once a new query exists.
- **Unmounting:** the user navigated away; no need to finish.
- **Race conditions:** an old slow response must never overwrite a newer one.
- **StrictMode:** the double effect run aborts the first request automatically.

### The pattern

Create the controller **inside** the effect, pass the signal, and abort in cleanup. In the `catch`, ignore `AbortError`; it is expected.

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  fetch(`/api/search?q=${q}`, { signal: controller.signal })
    .then(r => r.json()).then(setResults)
    .catch(e => { if (e.name !== "AbortError") setError(e); });
  return () => controller.abort();
}, [q]);
```

### Notes

- Aborting does not stop the **server** from working; it only closes the connection from the client side.
- axios accepts the same `signal` option.
- `AbortSignal.timeout(5000)` makes a signal that aborts after 5 s.
- For non-fetch async work, use an `ignore` boolean flag in cleanup.

topics.title: TanStack Query (React Query)
topics.summary: TanStack Query manages server state: caching, background refetching, retries, pagination and mutations.
topics.description:
Server data is different from UI state: it is **remote**, **shared**, can become **stale**, and needs caching and synchronization. Hand-written `useEffect` fetching does not solve that. **TanStack Query** (formerly React Query) is the standard library for **server state**.

### What you get for free

- **Caching** by query key and **deduplication** of identical requests.
- **Stale-while-revalidate**: show cached data instantly, refetch in the background.
- **Refetch** on window focus, reconnect, interval.
- **Retries** with backoff, `isPending`/`isError` flags.
- **Pagination** and **infinite queries**.
- **Mutations** with cache invalidation and optimistic updates.
- DevTools to inspect the cache.

### Core API

| API | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `QueryClientProvider` | provides the client at the app root |
| `useQuery({ queryKey, queryFn })` | read data |
| `useMutation({ mutationFn, onSuccess })` | create/update/delete |
| `queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey })` | mark stale and refetch |
| `useInfiniteQuery` | load more / infinite scroll |
| `useSuspenseQuery` | use with Suspense |

### Key concepts

- **queryKey** is the cache id: `["todos", { page }]`. Include every variable the function uses.
- **staleTime** (how long data is fresh) and **gcTime** (how long unused data stays in cache).
- Do not copy query data into `useState`; read it directly.

### With Redux?

You often do not need Redux for server data after adopting TanStack Query; keep Redux/Zustand for client UI state only.

topics.title: Pagination and Infinite Scroll
topics.summary: Load data in pages with page controls or a Load more button, and keep UI state tidy.
topics.description:
Never load thousands of records at once. Split data into pages.

### Pagination styles

| Style | How | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Page numbers** | `?page=3&limit=10` | admin tables, search results, bookmarkable pages |
| **Load more** | append next page | feeds with user control |
| **Infinite scroll** | auto-load near the bottom (IntersectionObserver) | social feeds |
| **Cursor-based** | `?after=<cursor>` | large or changing datasets |

### Implementation notes

- Keep `page` in state, or better in the **URL** (`useSearchParams`), so refresh and sharing work.
- Reset to page 1 when filters/search change.
- Disable Prev on the first page and Next on the last (`totalPages = Math.ceil(total / limit)`).
- Keep previous data visible while the next page loads (`placeholderData: keepPreviousData` in TanStack Query).
- For "load more" append results and track `hasMore`.
- Infinite scroll needs a **sentinel** element observed with `IntersectionObserver`, plus accessible alternatives and a way to reach the footer. Large lists need **virtualization**.
- `useInfiniteQuery` handles `pages`, `fetchNextPage` and `hasNextPage` for you.

### Offset vs cursor

Offset (`page`) is simple but can skip or duplicate items when data changes. Cursor pagination is stable and faster at depth, so most large APIs use it.

topics.title: Optimistic Updates
topics.summary: Update the UI immediately, then roll back if the server request fails.
topics.description:
Normally you click "Like", wait 400 ms for the server, and then the UI changes. With an **optimistic update** the UI changes instantly, assuming success, and rolls back if the request fails. The app feels fast.

### Recipe

1. **Snapshot** the current state.
2. **Apply** the change locally right away.
3. **Send** the request.
4. On **success** keep it (optionally replace with server data).
5. On **error** restore the snapshot and show a message.

### When it is a good idea

- Low-risk, high-success actions: like, toggle, reorder, rename, mark done.
- Not for payments or destructive operations where failure is likely or costly.

### Where it is implemented

- **TanStack Query:** `useMutation` with `onMutate` (snapshot + `setQueryData`), `onError` (restore from context) and `onSettled` (`invalidateQueries`).
- **React 19:** the `useOptimistic` hook shows temporary state during an Action.
- **Plain state:** like the example below.

### Edge cases

- Cancel in-flight queries before changing the cache to avoid being overwritten.
- Handle several fast clicks (queue or disable).
- Use temporary client ids for newly created items and swap with the server id after success.
- Always give users feedback on failure (toast + rollback).

topics.title: React Router Basics
topics.summary: React Router maps URLs to components so a single-page app can have multiple "pages" without reloads.
topics.description:
A single-page app (SPA) has one HTML file. **Client-side routing** changes what is rendered when the URL changes, using the History API, without a full page reload. **React Router** is the standard library. Version 6 introduced the current API; **version 7** merges it with Remix (import from `react-router`, with an optional framework mode) and keeps the same core ideas.

### Core pieces

| Piece | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `BrowserRouter` | enables routing with clean URLs |
| `Routes` / `Route` | match the URL to an `element` |
| `Link` | navigation without page reload (renders `<a>`) |
| `NavLink` | Link that knows if it is active (`isActive`) |
| `Navigate` | redirect declaratively |
| `path="*"` | catch-all, used for 404 pages |

### Setup

```jsx
import { BrowserRouter, Routes, Route, Link } from "react-router-dom";

<BrowserRouter>
  <nav><Link to="/">Home</Link> <Link to="/about">About</Link></nav>
  <Routes>
    <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
    <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
    <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
  </Routes>
</BrowserRouter>
```

### Notes

- Use `Link`, never a plain `<a href>`, for internal navigation (a plain anchor reloads the page).
- Routes match by **best specificity**, not order.
- Relative links resolve against the route they are rendered in.
- For static hosts, configure a **fallback to index.html** so refreshing `/about` does not return 404.
- `HashRouter` is an alternative for hosts without rewrite rules.

topics.title: Nested Routes and Layouts
topics.summary: Nest routes so shared layout (header, sidebar) stays while only the inner part changes, using Outlet.
topics.description:
Real apps share layouts: a navbar and footer on every page, a sidebar on dashboard pages. Nested routes express this directly in the route tree.

```jsx
<Routes>
  <Route element={<MainLayout />}>
    <Route index element={<Home />} />
    <Route path="products" element={<Products />} />
    <Route path="dashboard" element={<DashboardLayout />}>
      <Route index element={<Overview />} />
      <Route path="settings" element={<Settings />} />
    </Route>
  </Route>
  <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
</Routes>
```

### Outlet

A parent route renders `<Outlet />` where its matched child should appear:

```jsx
function MainLayout() {
  return (
    <>
      <Header />
      <main><Outlet /></main>
      <Footer />
    </>
  );
}
```

### Concepts

- **Layout routes**: a route with no `path` (only `element`) used purely for layout and shared logic.
- **Index routes**: `index` renders at the parent's exact URL.
- **Relative paths**: child `path="settings"` becomes `/dashboard/settings`.
- **Outlet context**: `<Outlet context={...} />` passes data to children via `useOutletContext()`.
- **Pathless routes** group routes for guards without changing the URL.

### Benefits

State inside the layout is preserved while navigating between its children, and you avoid duplicating headers in every page component.

topics.title: Params, Search Params and Navigation
topics.summary: Read URL parameters with useParams, query strings with useSearchParams, and navigate in code with useNavigate.
topics.description:
URLs carry state. React Router gives hooks to read and change it.

### Dynamic segments - `useParams`

```jsx
<Route path="/users/:userId" element={<User />} />

function User() {
  const { userId } = useParams();   // always a string!
}
```

Convert numbers yourself: `Number(userId)`. Optional segments use `:id?` and splats use `*`.

### Query string - `useSearchParams`

```jsx
const [params, setParams] = useSearchParams();
const q = params.get("q") ?? "";
setParams({ q: "react", page: "2" });
```

It works like `useState`, but the state lives in the URL, so it survives refresh and can be shared. Ideal for filters, search, sorting and pagination.

### Programmatic navigation - `useNavigate`

```jsx
const navigate = useNavigate();
navigate("/orders/42");
navigate(-1);                       // back
navigate("/login", { replace: true, state: { from: location } });
```

Use it after forms or login. Use `<Navigate to="/login" replace />` when you want to redirect during render.

### Location and state

`useLocation()` returns `pathname`, `search`, `hash` and `state` (data passed through `navigate`, not visible in URL).

### Tips

- Prefer `Link` for normal navigation; use `navigate` for side-effect-driven moves.
- `replace` avoids filling the back-button history with redirects.

topics.title: Data Routers: Loaders and Actions
topics.summary: Fetch data before rendering a route and handle form submissions with loader and action functions.
topics.description:
The **data router** API (`createBrowserRouter` + `RouterProvider`) lets a route declare its data needs next to its path. This avoids "render, then fetch in an effect, then show spinner" waterfalls.

```jsx
const router = createBrowserRouter([
  {
    path: "/",
    element: <Root />,
    errorElement: <ErrorPage />,
    children: [
      {
        path: "posts/:id",
        loader: ({ params }) => fetch(`/api/posts/${params.id}`).then(r => r.json()),
        action: async ({ request }) => { /* handle form POST */ },
        element: <Post />,
      },
    ],
  },
]);
<RouterProvider router={router} />
```

### Pieces

- **`loader`** - runs before the route renders (in parallel for nested routes). Read in the component with `useLoaderData()`.
- **`action`** - handles `<Form method="post">` submissions and `fetcher.submit`. After an action, loaders **revalidate** automatically so the UI stays in sync.
- **`errorElement`** - renders if the loader, action or component throws. Read the error with `useRouteError()`.
- **`useNavigation()`** - `state` is `idle | loading | submitting` for global progress bars.
- **`useFetcher()`** - call loaders/actions without navigating (like buttons, inline edits).
- **`defer` / `Await`** (v6) or streaming promises (v7) - render fast parts first.

### Why use it

Parallel data loading, built-in error handling, no spinners-in-spinners, and automatic revalidation after mutations. In React Router v7 framework mode it adds SSR, type-safe loaders and file-based or config routes.

### With TanStack Query

You can call `queryClient.ensureQueryData` inside a loader to combine caching with route-level fetching.
