topics.title: Protected Routes and Auth Redirects
topics.summary: Guard routes by checking authentication and redirect unauthenticated users to login, remembering where they wanted to go.
topics.description:
Some pages (dashboard, profile, checkout) require a logged-in user. A **protected route** is a wrapper that checks auth and either renders the page or redirects.

### Pattern: guard layout route

```jsx
function RequireAuth() {
  const { user, loading } = useAuth();
  const location = useLocation();

  if (loading) return <Spinner />;               // still checking session
  if (!user) return <Navigate to="/login" replace state={{ from: location }} />;
  return <Outlet />;                              // render child routes
}

<Route element={<RequireAuth />}>
  <Route path="/dashboard" element={<Dashboard />} />
  <Route path="/profile" element={<Profile />} />
</Route>
```

### After login

Read `location.state?.from` and `navigate(from, { replace: true })` so users land where they were headed.

### Details that matter

- **Loading state:** on refresh the auth status is unknown for a moment. Show a spinner; otherwise logged-in users are bounced to login.
- **Role-based access:** `RequireRole role="admin"` renders 403 or redirects.
- **Public-only routes:** redirect logged-in users away from `/login`.
- **Store auth in a context** (`AuthProvider` with `useAuth`), initialize from a cookie/session check.

### Security reminder

Route guards are only **UX**. Anyone can read your JavaScript bundle. Real protection is on the **server**: every API call must verify the token/session and permissions. Prefer HttpOnly cookies for session tokens over localStorage.

### 404 and error pages

- `path="*"` for unknown URLs.
- In the data router use `errorElement` for thrown errors; throw `new Response("Not found", { status: 404 })` from loaders for missing resources.
- Show a friendly page with a link home. Remember the server should also return a 404 status for SSR apps.

### Scroll and focus

- SPA navigation does not reset scroll. Use `<ScrollRestoration />` (data routers) or a small effect that scrolls to top on `pathname` change.
- Move focus to the main heading after navigation for screen reader users and update `document.title`.

### Prefetching

Call the import function on link hover (`onMouseEnter={() => import("./pages/Dashboard")}`) for instant navigation. React Router v7 `<Link prefetch="intent">` does this in framework mode.

topics.title: Redux Toolkit: Store and Slices
topics.summary: Redux Toolkit is the modern, low-boilerplate way to use Redux for predictable global state.
topics.description:
**Redux** keeps application state in one **store** and changes it through dispatched **actions** handled by pure **reducers**. The classic setup was verbose; **Redux Toolkit (RTK)** is now the official, recommended way to write Redux.

### The data flow

1. A component dispatches an action: `dispatch(addTodo("Buy milk"))`.
2. The reducer computes the new state.
3. The store notifies subscribers; `useSelector` re-renders components whose selected data changed.

### RTK building blocks

| API | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `configureStore` | creates the store (DevTools and thunk included) |
| `createSlice` | defines name, initial state, reducers; generates action creators |
| `Provider` | gives the store to React |
| `useSelector(fn)` | read a piece of state |
| `useDispatch()` | get `dispatch` |
| `createAsyncThunk` | async logic with pending/fulfilled/rejected actions |
| `createSelector` | memoized derived data |

### Immer inside

Inside `createSlice` reducers you may **write "mutating" code** (`state.items.push(x)`). Immer turns it into an immutable update behind the scenes. Outside slices, still treat state as immutable.

### Good practices

- Keep state **serializable** (no functions, class instances, Dates).
- Store the minimum; derive the rest with selectors.
- One slice per feature (`features/cart/cartSlice.js`).
- Select small pieces (`state => state.cart.items.length`) to reduce re-renders.
- Use typed hooks (`useAppSelector`) with TypeScript.
- Don't put form field state or local UI toggles in Redux.

topics.title: Zustand
topics.summary: Zustand is a tiny hook-based global store with no providers and almost no boilerplate.
topics.description:
**Zustand** (German for "state") is a minimalist state library. You create a store with `create`, and it returns a hook. No Provider, no reducers, no action types required.

```js
import { create } from "zustand";

const useCart = create((set, get) => ({
  items: [],
  add: (item) => set((s) => ({ items: [...s.items, item] })),
  clear: () => set({ items: [] }),
  total: () => get().items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0),
}));
```

### Using it

```jsx
const count = useCart((s) => s.items.length);   // selector
const add = useCart((s) => s.add);
```

Passing a **selector** means the component re-renders only when that slice changes. Selecting the whole store re-renders on every change.

### Features

- Works outside React (`useCart.getState()`, `useCart.setState()`, `subscribe`).
- Middleware: `persist` (localStorage), `devtools` (Redux DevTools), `immer`.
- Async actions are just async functions that call `set`.
- Very small (~1 KB) and fast; built on `useSyncExternalStore`.
- `useShallow` selects multiple fields without extra renders.

### Compared with Redux

Less ceremony and learning curve, flexible structure. Redux gives stricter conventions, richer DevTools and RTK Query, which suits very large teams.

### Tips

- Split the store into slices by feature for big apps.
- Keep actions inside the store next to the data.
- Don't use it for server cache; use TanStack Query for that.

topics.title: Jotai, Recoil and Atomic State
topics.summary: Atomic libraries model state as small independent atoms that components subscribe to individually.
topics.description:
**Atomic state management** splits global state into many small pieces called **atoms**. A component subscribes only to the atoms it uses, so updates are precise. Derived values are separate atoms computed from others.

### Jotai

Minimal, ~3 KB, API like `useState`.

```jsx
import { atom, useAtom, useAtomValue } from "jotai";

const countAtom = atom(0);
const doubleAtom = atom((get) => get(countAtom) * 2);   // derived atom

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useAtom(countAtom);
  const double = useAtomValue(doubleAtom);
}
```

Strengths: no Provider needed (optional for scoping), great TypeScript, async atoms with Suspense, `atomWithStorage`, small and active.

### Recoil

Created by Meta with `atom`, `selector`, `useRecoilState`, `RecoilRoot`. It popularized atomic state but the repository was **archived** (development stopped), so new projects should prefer **Jotai** (similar model) or Zustand.

### Other options

| Library | Style |
| --- | --- |
| **Valtio** | proxy-based, mutate objects, auto-tracking |
| **MobX** | observable objects and reactions |
| **XState Store** | event-driven stores and machines |
| **Nanostores** | tiny framework-agnostic atoms |

### When atoms shine

Many independent pieces of state, dynamic or derived state graphs, fine-grained re-render control, and code-splitting state with components.

topics.title: Choosing State Management: Context vs Redux vs Zustand
topics.summary: Pick tools by the kind of state: local, shared UI, server cache, URL, forms.
topics.description:
There is no single "best" state library. First classify the state, then pick the simplest tool.

### Kinds of state

| Kind | Examples | Best tool |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Local UI** | modal open, input text | `useState` / `useReducer` |
| **Shared UI (few components)** | selected tab, wizard step | lift state up |
| **Global client state** | theme, cart, auth user, sidebar | Context, Zustand, Redux, Jotai |
| **Server state** | users, products, orders | **TanStack Query / RTK Query** |
| **URL state** | filters, page, sort | router search params |
| **Form state** | values, errors, touched | React Hook Form |

### Decision guide

- **Context + hooks:** small apps, low-frequency data (theme, locale, auth). No extra dependency. Beware re-renders of all consumers.
- **Zustand / Jotai:** medium apps, need selectors and little boilerplate.
- **Redux Toolkit:** large teams, strict structure, middleware, time-travel debugging, complex workflows, RTK Query.
- **TanStack Query:** whenever data comes from a server. This removes most "global state".

### Rules of thumb

1. Start with local state. Lift only when needed.
2. Don't put server data into a client store; use a cache library.
3. Don't keep derived data; compute it.
4. Keep state as close to where it is used as possible.
5. Avoid one giant global store for everything.

### Migration is easy

Because components access state through hooks, you can swap Context for Zustand later without redesigning the UI.

topics.title: CSS, Inline Styles and CSS Modules
topics.summary: Style React with plain CSS files, inline style objects or locally scoped CSS Modules.
topics.description:
React does not force a styling method. The common options are:

### 1. Plain CSS files

Import a stylesheet (`import "./App.css"`) and use `className`. Simple, but CSS is **global**: a `.button` class in one file can clash with another.

### 2. Inline styles

`style={{ color: "red", fontSize: 18 }}` takes an object with camelCase properties; numbers get `px`. Good for **dynamic values** (progress width, computed colors). Limitations: no pseudo-classes (`:hover`), no media queries, no keyframes, and they have high specificity.

### 3. CSS Modules

Name the file `Button.module.css`. The bundler turns each class into a unique name, so styles are **scoped to the component**.

```jsx
import styles from "./Button.module.css";
<button className={styles.primary}>Save</button>
```

You write ordinary CSS, get no collisions, and need no runtime library. Compose with `composes:`, and use `:global(...)` for exceptions. Vite supports CSS Modules out of the box.

### Combining class names

Use the tiny **`clsx`** (or `classnames`) helper:

```jsx
className={clsx(styles.btn, isActive && styles.active, disabled && styles.disabled)}
```

### Choosing

CSS Modules are a safe, fast default. Plain CSS plus a naming convention (BEM) works for small apps. Reach for utility CSS (Tailwind) or CSS-in-JS if your team prefers them.

### Tips

Use CSS variables for design tokens, keep responsive rules in the stylesheet, and avoid mixing several approaches in one project without a reason.

topics.title: Tailwind CSS with React
topics.summary: Tailwind provides small utility classes you compose in JSX instead of writing custom CSS.
topics.description:
**Tailwind CSS** is a utility-first framework. Instead of naming classes and writing CSS, you apply tiny single-purpose classes directly in `className`.

```jsx
<button className="rounded-lg bg-sky-500 px-4 py-2 font-semibold text-white hover:bg-sky-600 focus:outline-none focus:ring-2 md:px-6">
  Save
</button>
```

### How it works

Tailwind scans your source files, finds the class names you used, and generates only that CSS. The production CSS file is usually only a few kilobytes. In v4 setup is just `@import "tailwindcss";` plus the Vite plugin `@tailwindcss/vite`; earlier versions use `tailwind.config.js` and PostCSS.

### Why developers like it

- No context switching between files; no naming problems.
- **Design constraints** (spacing, colors, font sizes) keep UI consistent.
- **Responsive and state variants** are built-in: `md:`, `lg:`, `hover:`, `focus:`, `disabled:`, `dark:`, `group-hover:`.
- Zero runtime and works with Server Components.

### Handling long class lists

- Extract **React components** (`<Button variant="primary" />`), not CSS classes, to reuse styles.
- Use `clsx`/`tailwind-merge` (`cn()` helper) to merge conditional and overriding classes.
- Use **cva** (class-variance-authority) for variants. shadcn/ui follows this approach.

### Dark mode

Add `dark:` variants; enable by class (`.dark` on `<html>`) or system preference.

### Pitfalls

Never build class names dynamically (`bg-${color}-500`): the scanner can't see them. Use complete strings in a lookup object.

topics.title: CSS-in-JS Trade-offs and Choosing a Styling Strategy
topics.summary: Compare runtime CSS-in-JS, CSS Modules, utility CSS and zero-runtime solutions.
topics.description:
Every approach trades something. Here is a practical comparison.

| Approach | Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Plain CSS / BEM** | simple, fast, standard | global scope, naming discipline |
| **CSS Modules** | scoped, no runtime, real CSS | dynamic styles need CSS variables/inline |
| **Tailwind** | fast to build, consistent, zero runtime | verbose markup, learning the classes |
| **Runtime CSS-in-JS** (styled-components, Emotion) | colocated, dynamic props, theming | runtime cost, bundle size, SSR/RSC complexity |
| **Zero-runtime CSS-in-JS** (vanilla-extract, Panda, StyleX, Linaria) | typed, scoped, no runtime | build tooling, less dynamic |
| **Component libraries** (MUI, Chakra, shadcn/ui, Mantine) | ready components, accessibility | opinionated look, bundle size, customization limits |

### Why runtime CSS-in-JS lost ground

- It serializes styles and injects `<style>` tags while rendering, adding **CPU work on every render** and slowing hydration.
- React 18 concurrent rendering and **Server Components** do not mix well with context-based style injection.
- Larger JS bundles.

### Dynamic styles without runtime CSS-in-JS

Use **CSS custom properties**: set `style={{ "--progress": value + "%" }}` and in CSS `width: var(--progress)`. You get dynamic values with static CSS.

### How to choose

- New project, performance sensitive, or Next.js App Router: **CSS Modules or Tailwind** (optionally shadcn/ui).
- Large design system with strict typing: **vanilla-extract / Panda / StyleX**.
- Existing styled-components code: keep it; migrate gradually if needed.
- Prototype fast: **a component library**.

Whatever you pick, define **design tokens** (colors, spacing, radii) once and respect accessibility (contrast, focus styles, reduced motion).

topics.title: Theming and Dark Mode
topics.summary: Implement light/dark themes with CSS variables, a data attribute and a small context, respecting user preference.
topics.description:
A solid theming setup has three parts.

### 1. Design tokens as CSS variables

```css
:root { --bg: #ffffff; --text: #111827; --primary: #0ea5e9; }
[data-theme="dark"] { --bg: #0f172a; --text: #e5e7eb; --primary: #38bdf8; }
body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--text); }
```

Components use `var(--primary)`. Switching the theme only changes the attribute, with no re-render of the tree.

### 2. State and persistence

Keep the theme in a React context (`ThemeProvider` + `useTheme`). Initialize from `localStorage`, otherwise from `window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)")`. Support three values: `light`, `dark`, `system`.

### 3. Apply to the document

In an effect set `document.documentElement.dataset.theme = theme` and save to storage.

### Avoiding the flash (FOUC)

If the theme is applied only after React hydrates, users see a flash of the wrong theme. Add a tiny **inline script in `index.html`** `<head>` that reads storage and sets the attribute **before** first paint.

### With Tailwind / UI libraries

Tailwind: `darkMode: "class"` and `dark:` variants. MUI and Chakra: provide their theme providers.

### Accessibility

Keep contrast ratios in both themes, use `color-scheme: light dark` so native controls match, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.

        var theme = saved || (dark ? "dark" : "light");
        document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", theme);

topics.title: The Rendering Model: When and Why Components Re-render
topics.summary: Understand triggers, render vs commit, and why a parent re-render re-renders its children.
topics.description:
You cannot optimize what you do not understand. React work happens in three phases: **trigger -> render -> commit**.

### What triggers a render

1. The **initial render** (`root.render`).
2. A **state update** in the component (`setState`, `dispatch`).
3. A **parent re-render** (children re-render by default, even if their props are identical).
4. A **context** value change for components that consume it.

Props changing is not the trigger; the parent rendering is. `memo` is what adds the props comparison.

### Render phase

React calls your component function and builds the new element tree. It must be **pure** (same props/state -> same JSX, no side effects). Rendering is cheap if components are small, but can be costly for huge trees or expensive calculations.

### Commit phase

React applies the minimum DOM changes, runs layout effects, then the browser paints, then passive effects (`useEffect`) run. If a render produces the same output, the DOM is not touched. **A re-render is not a DOM update.**

### Batching and priority

Updates in the same tick are batched. Transitions (`startTransition`) are interruptible low-priority renders.

### Common misconceptions

- "Re-rendering is always bad." Usually it is fine; measure first.
- "Props changes cause re-render." The parent's render does; `memo` stops it.
- "Setting state to the same value re-renders." React bails out (may render the component once more but not the children).

### Where cost really comes from

Large lists, expensive calculations in render, deep trees re-rendering from high-up state, and huge DOM sizes.

interview.a: No. React diffs the output and only changes the DOM where something differs.

Apply these in order, from cheapest to most complex. ### 1. Colocate state (move state down) If only `` needs the typed text, keep that state **inside** it, not in the big parent. Now typing re-renders only the small component. ### 2. Lift content up (the children trick) Pass expensive subtrees as `children` or props. They are created by a parent that does not re-render when the wrapper's state changes: ```jsx function Wrapper({ children }) { const [x, setX] = useState(0); // changes often return
{children}
; // children element is unchanged } ``` ### 3. Avoid expensive work in render Move calculations out of the component, or `useMemo` them if measurably slow. Paginate or filter data early. ### 4. memo + stable props Wrap an expensive component in `memo` **and** ensure props are stable: primitives, `useMemo` objects, `useCallback` handlers. If even one prop is a fresh object each render, memo is wasted. ### 5. Split context Separate frequently changing values from stable ones, or use a store with selectors. ### 6. Fix keys and list size Stable keys, virtualization for long lists. ### 7. Reduce update frequency Debounce, throttle, `useDeferredValue`, `startTransition`. ### Measure Use the React DevTools Profiler ("Why did this render?") and `console.time`. Optimization that is not measured is a guess. With the **React Compiler**, step 4 largely disappears.

Row {index}

topics.title: Code Splitting and Bundle Analysis
topics.summary: Ship less JavaScript: split by route, lazy load heavy features and inspect the bundle with a visualizer.
topics.description:
JavaScript is the most expensive resource per byte: it must be downloaded, parsed and executed. Reducing the initial bundle improves Largest Contentful Paint and interactivity.

### Code splitting strategies

1. **Route-based**: `lazy(() => import("./pages/Admin"))` per page (biggest win).
2. **Component-based**: heavy widgets (charts, editors, maps, PDF viewers) loaded when needed.
3. **Library-based**: dynamic `import("xlsx")` inside the click handler that needs it.
4. **Vendor chunks**: Vite/Rollup `manualChunks` to cache stable libraries separately.
5. **Prefetch/preload** next likely chunks on hover or idle.

### Find the weight: analyze the bundle

- **`rollup-plugin-visualizer`** (Vite): generates a treemap `stats.html`.
- **webpack-bundle-analyzer** for webpack.
- Chrome DevTools **Coverage** tab shows unused code; **Lighthouse** gives guidance.
- `source-map-explorer` for source maps.

### Common wins

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Moment.js with all locales | use `date-fns` / `dayjs` |
| `import _ from "lodash"` | `import debounce from "lodash/debounce"` or `lodash-es` |
| Huge icon pack | import individual icons |
| Large images | modern formats (WebP/AVIF), `loading="lazy"`, correct sizes |
| Duplicate libs/versions | dedupe with the package manager |

### Tree shaking

Use ES module imports and libraries with `sideEffects: false`; avoid barrel files that pull in everything.

### Budgets

Set a performance budget (e.g. under 170 KB gzipped initial JS) and fail CI when exceeded.

topics.title: Profiling with React DevTools
topics.summary: Record renders in the Profiler tab to see what rendered, why, and how long it took.
topics.description:
Measure before you optimize. React gives two tools.

### React DevTools Profiler

Install the **React Developer Tools** browser extension. In the **Profiler** tab:

1. Click **Record**.
2. Interact with the app (type, click).
3. Click **Stop**.

You get a **flamegraph** (each bar a component, width = render time, gray = did not render) and a **ranked chart** of slowest components. Enable "**Record why each component rendered**" in settings to see reasons: *props changed*, *state changed*, *hooks changed*, *parent rendered*, *context changed*.

The **Components** tab has "Highlight updates when components render", which flashes re-rendering components.

### Always profile a production build

Development mode is much slower (StrictMode double renders, extra checks). Use `npm run build && npm run preview` for real numbers, or the profiling build.

### The `<Profiler>` component

Programmatic measurement:

```jsx
<Profiler id="Feed" onRender={(id, phase, actualDuration) => log(id, phase, actualDuration)}>
  <Feed />
</Profiler>
```

`phase` is `"mount"` or `"update"`; `actualDuration` is time spent rendering. Useful for logging metrics.

### Other tools

- Chrome **Performance** panel for long tasks and layout thrash.
- **Lighthouse** and **Web Vitals** (LCP, INP, CLS).
- `why-did-you-render` library for development.

### Workflow

Reproduce slow interaction -> record -> find the expensive or unnecessarily re-rendering component -> fix -> record again to confirm.

topics.title: React Compiler Overview
topics.summary: The React Compiler automatically memoizes components and values at build time so manual memo/useMemo/useCallback are rarely needed.
topics.description:
Manual memoization (`memo`, `useMemo`, `useCallback`) is noisy and easy to get wrong. The **React Compiler** (formerly "React Forget"), stable as of React 19-era tooling (v1.0), is a build-time Babel/SWC plugin that analyzes your components and **automatically inserts memoization** where it is safe.

### What it does

- Understands the **Rules of React** (pure render, immutable state and props, hooks rules).
- Splits your component into cached pieces so JSX and values are reused if their inputs did not change.
- Even memoizes things that hooks cannot, such as values after early returns.
- Works with React 17, 18 and 19 (via `react-compiler-runtime`).

### Setup (Vite)

```bash
npm i -D babel-plugin-react-compiler
```

```js
// vite.config.js
react({ babel: { plugins: [["babel-plugin-react-compiler", {}]] } })
```

Frameworks (Next.js `experimental.reactCompiler`, Expo) have flags. Run **`npx react-compiler-healthcheck`** to see how much of your code is compatible and use the `eslint-plugin-react-compiler` / `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` rules to find violations.

### What changes for you

- Write plain code; drop most `useMemo`/`useCallback`/`memo`.
- Keep manual memo where you need exact control, such as stable effect dependencies.
- Components breaking the rules are **skipped** (not broken), and you can opt out with `"use no memo"`.
- DevTools shows a "Memo" badge for compiled components.

### Caveats

It will not fix algorithmic problems, big lists or network waterfalls. Mutating props/state or reading refs in render makes components ineligible.

topics.title: Web Performance Checklist for React Apps
topics.summary: A practical checklist covering loading speed, rendering, images, network and Core Web Vitals.
topics.description:
Use this checklist when an app feels slow.

### Loading (LCP, bundle)

- Route-level code splitting and lazy loading.
- Analyze the bundle; remove or replace heavy libraries.
- Compress with gzip/Brotli; serve from a CDN with long-term caching (hashed filenames).
- Preload critical resources (`<link rel="preload">` for fonts and hero image), `preconnect` to API origins.
- Consider **SSR/SSG** (Next.js) for content pages so HTML arrives ready.

### Images and fonts

- Modern formats, correct dimensions, `srcset`, `loading="lazy"` below the fold, `width`/`height` to avoid layout shift (CLS).
- `font-display: swap`, subset fonts, self-host.

### Rendering and interactivity (INP)

- Keep state local, avoid unnecessary re-renders (see optimization topic).
- Virtualize long lists; paginate.
- Debounce inputs; use `startTransition` / `useDeferredValue` for heavy updates.
- Avoid long tasks (> 50 ms): split work, use Web Workers for CPU-heavy code.
- Avoid layout thrashing (reading and writing layout in loops).

### Network

- Cache with TanStack Query; dedupe and prefetch.
- Request only needed fields/pages; use HTTP caching headers.
- Avoid request waterfalls: parallelize with `Promise.all`, load data at the route level.

### Measure

| Metric | Good |
| --- | --- |
| LCP | <= 2.5 s |
| INP | <= 200 ms |
| CLS | <= 0.1 |

Use Lighthouse, PageSpeed Insights, the `web-vitals` package and real-user monitoring.

topics.title: Testing Strategy and Vitest/Jest Setup
topics.summary: Test behavior the way users see it; use Vitest (or Jest) with jsdom and React Testing Library.
topics.description:
Good tests give confidence to change code. The popular React stack is:

- **Test runner:** **Vitest** (fast, Vite-native, Jest-compatible API) or **Jest**.
- **Environment:** `jsdom` (or `happy-dom`) to simulate a browser.
- **Library:** **React Testing Library (RTL)** to render and query components.
- **Helpers:** `@testing-library/user-event`, `@testing-library/jest-dom` (matchers like `toBeInTheDocument`), **MSW** for network mocks.

### What to test

Follow the **testing trophy**: mostly integration tests, some unit, few end-to-end.

| Level | Example | Tools |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | reducers, utils, hooks | Vitest/Jest |
| Component / integration | form submit shows error | RTL |
| End-to-end | login -> checkout | Playwright / Cypress |

### Principle

> The more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you.

Test **what the user sees and does** (text, roles, labels, clicks), not implementation details (state variables, method names, CSS classes).

### Vitest setup

```js
// vite.config.js
test: { environment: "jsdom", globals: true, setupFiles: "./src/test/setup.js" }
```

```js
// src/test/setup.js
import "@testing-library/jest-dom/vitest";
import { afterEach } from "vitest";
import { cleanup } from "@testing-library/react";
afterEach(cleanup);
```

### Tips

- Keep tests independent and deterministic (fake timers, mocked network).
- Name tests as behaviors: "shows an error when email is invalid".
- Aim for meaningful coverage, not 100% numbers.

RTL renders your component into jsdom and gives queries that mimic how users and assistive tech find things.

### Query families

| Prefix | Throws if missing? | Async? | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `getBy...` | yes | no | element must exist now |
| `queryBy...` | no (returns null) | no | assert element is absent |
| `findBy...` | yes | yes (waits) | element appears later |
| `getAllBy`, `queryAllBy`, `findAllBy` | | | multiple elements |

### Query priority (best to worst)

1. `getByRole("button", { name: /save/i })` - what screen readers see.
2. `getByLabelText("Email")` - form fields.
3. `getByPlaceholderText`, `getByText`, `getByDisplayValue`.
4. `getByAltText`, `getByTitle`.
5. `getByTestId` - last resort.

### Matchers from jest-dom

`toBeInTheDocument()`, `toBeVisible()`, `toBeDisabled()`, `toHaveTextContent()`, `toHaveValue()`, `toHaveAttribute()`, `toBeChecked()`.

### Other helpers

- `screen` - queries bound to `document.body`; prefer it over destructuring `render`.
- `within(element)` - scope queries.
- `waitFor(() => expect(...))` - retry an assertion until it passes.
- `renderHook` - test custom hooks.
- Wrap in providers via a custom `render` helper (Router, QueryClient, theme).

### Debugging

`screen.debug()` prints the DOM and `screen.logTestingPlaygroundURL()` suggests the best query.

topics.title: user-event and Async Testing
topics.summary: Simulate realistic user interactions with user-event and wait for async updates correctly.
topics.description:
`fireEvent` dispatches a single DOM event. **`@testing-library/user-event`** simulates what a real user does: typing triggers focus, keydown, input and keyup events for each character, clicking triggers hover, mouse down/up and click, and it respects disabled state and pointer rules.

### Usage

```js
const user = userEvent.setup();     // create once per test
await user.click(button);
await user.type(input, "hello{enter}");
await user.clear(input);
await user.selectOptions(select, "red");
await user.tab();
await user.keyboard("{Escape}");
```

All methods are **async** - always `await` them.

### Async UI

When something appears after a promise or timer:

- **`await screen.findByText(...)`** - waits (default 1000 ms).
- **`await waitFor(() => expect(fn).toHaveBeenCalled())`** - retries the callback.
- **`await waitForElementToBeRemoved(() => screen.queryByText("Loading..."))`**.

Do not put side effects (clicks) in `waitFor`, and avoid arbitrary `sleep`.

### Fake timers

For debounce/polling: `vi.useFakeTimers()` then `await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(500)`. With user-event pass `userEvent.setup({ advanceTimers: vi.advanceTimersByTime })`.

### Mock functions

`const onSubmit = vi.fn()` and `expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ email: "a@b.com" })` test callbacks from props.

### act warnings

RTL wraps interactions in `act` for you. "not wrapped in act" warnings usually mean you forgot to `await` a user-event call or an async update after the test ended.

topics.title: Mocking APIs: vi.fn, fetch mocks and MSW
topics.summary: Mock network requests at the network boundary with Mock Service Worker for realistic tests.
topics.description:
Tests should not hit real servers: they are slow, flaky and may change data. There are three levels of mocking.

### 1. Mock the function

`vi.mock("./api")` replaces a module, and `vi.spyOn(global, "fetch").mockResolvedValue(...)` replaces fetch. Quick, but tied to **how** you call the API.

### 2. Mock the network with MSW

**MSW (Mock Service Worker)** intercepts requests at the network level (in Node via `msw/node`; in the browser via a service worker). Your component code runs unchanged with `fetch` or axios.

```js
import { http, HttpResponse } from "msw";
import { setupServer } from "msw/node";

export const server = setupServer(
  http.get("/api/users", () => HttpResponse.json([{ id: 1, name: "Asha" }]))
);
```

Lifecycle in the setup file:

```js
beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: "error" }));
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());
```

Override per test: `server.use(http.get("/api/users", () => new HttpResponse(null, { status: 500 })))` to test error states.

### Why MSW

- Same mocks for unit tests, Storybook and local development.
- Tests exercise your real fetching code, including headers and error handling.
- Refactoring from fetch to axios does not break tests.

### Tips

- Test loading, success, empty and error states.
- With TanStack Query create a **new QueryClient per test** with `retry: false`.
- Keep mock data factories (faker) in one place.

topics.title: Concurrent Rendering and Automatic Batching
topics.summary: React 18 can prepare renders in the background and interrupt them, and it batches all state updates automatically.
topics.description:
React 18 introduced **concurrent rendering**. It is not a feature you switch on; it is a new engine capability that powers `useTransition`, `useDeferredValue` and Suspense improvements. You opt in simply by using `createRoot` instead of the old `ReactDOM.render`.

### What "concurrent" means

In legacy React, once rendering began it could not be stopped, so a long render blocked the main thread (typing froze). In concurrent mode React can **start rendering, pause, handle something urgent, and resume or discard** the old work. Rendering becomes interruptible, but is still **single-threaded** (it is time slicing, not multi-threading).

### Update priorities

- **Urgent**: typing, clicking, pressing - must feel instant.
- **Transition**: view changes and filtering - may be delayed (`startTransition`).
- React always keeps the urgent updates responsive.

### Automatic batching

Before React 18, only updates inside React event handlers were batched. Updates in `setTimeout`, promises or native event handlers caused one render **per** `setState`. In React 18+ **all** updates are batched, wherever they happen:

```js
setTimeout(() => {
  setCount(c => c + 1);
  setFlag(f => !f);
  // one re-render, not two
}, 1000);
```

If you truly need immediate DOM updates between calls, wrap one in `flushSync(() => setState(...))` from `react-dom` (rare).

### Other React 18 additions

`useId`, `useSyncExternalStore`, `useInsertionEffect`, streaming SSR with `<Suspense>`, selective hydration, StrictMode double-effects.

### Migration note

Use `createRoot(container).render(<App />)`. Code must be pure and effects must clean up, because concurrent rendering can call render more than once.

topics.title: Suspense for Data Fetching
topics.summary: Components can "suspend" while waiting for data; Suspense boundaries show fallbacks and coordinate loading UI.
topics.description:
Suspense began with lazy code loading. In React 18/19 it also works for **data**: a component that is not ready can **suspend**, and the nearest `<Suspense fallback>` displays a loading UI until it is ready.

### How it works

A Suspense-enabled data source *throws a promise* during render when the data is missing. React catches it, shows the fallback, and re-renders when the promise resolves. You normally never throw promises yourself; you use:

- **TanStack Query** `useSuspenseQuery`
- **Relay**, **SWR** (suspense mode)
- Framework loaders (Next.js, React Router, Remix)
- React 19's **`use(promise)`** hook
- Server Components with `async`/`await`

### Benefits

- No `isLoading` checks in every component: write the happy path.
- **Declarative loading states**: decide at the boundary where spinners appear.
- Avoids waterfalls when siblings fetch in parallel.
- **Streaming SSR**: the server sends HTML in chunks as Suspense boundaries resolve.

### Design tips

- Several small boundaries beat one global spinner: parts of the page can appear independently.
- Nest boundaries to define a loading hierarchy (page skeleton, then widgets).
- Pair with an **error boundary** for failures.
- Use `startTransition`/`useDeferredValue` so existing content stays visible instead of flipping back to a fallback.
- **Create the promise outside render** (in a cache or loader) to avoid refetching every render.

{c.text}

); } }> ``` While the promise is pending, the component suspends and the nearest Suspense fallback is shown. If it rejects, the nearest error boundary catches it. ### Reading context `use(ThemeContext)` works like `useContext`, but **can be called after early returns or inside conditions and loops** - a first for a hook-like API. ```jsx function Button({ show }) { if (!show) return null; const theme = use(ThemeContext); // allowed } ``` ### Promise rules - Pass the promise **from a parent / Server Component / cache**. Creating `use(fetch(...))` directly in a Client Component render creates a new promise each time and React warns. - In Server Components prefer `async/await`; for Client Components pass the promise as a prop (streamed from the server). - `use` can't be used in try/catch for the promise; use an error boundary or `.catch` on the promise. ### Why it matters It simplifies data loading (no `useEffect` + state), unlocks streaming from server to client and replaces `useContext` in conditional code.

topics.summary: React 19 simplifies refs and context, supports document metadata and improves error reporting and custom elements.

Besides Actions, React 19 (December 2024) brings many quality-of-life changes.

### `ref` as a regular prop

Function components receive `ref` like any prop - **no `forwardRef` needed**:

```jsx
function MyInput({ placeholder, ref }) {
  return <input placeholder={placeholder} ref={ref} />;
}
```

`forwardRef` still works but will be deprecated. **Ref callbacks can return a cleanup function**.

### Context as a provider

`<ThemeContext value="dark">` replaces `<ThemeContext.Provider value="dark">`.

### Document metadata

Render `<title>`, `<meta>` and `<link>` anywhere in your components; React hoists them to `<head>`. Stylesheets with `precedence` and `<script async>` are deduplicated.

### Resource preloading APIs

`preload`, `preinit`, `prefetchDNS`, `preconnect` from `react-dom` to hint the browser early.

### Better errors and hydration

- Errors are reported once (`onCaughtError`, `onUncaughtError` root options).
- Clear **hydration mismatch diffs** and support for third-party scripts that edit `<head>`/`<body>`.

### Other changes

- **Custom Elements** (Web Components) fully supported.
- **Cleanup of `defaultProps`** for function components (use default parameters) and removal of `propTypes`, `string refs`, legacy context and `ReactDOM.render` / `hydrate` (use `createRoot`/`hydrateRoot`).
- `useDeferredValue` accepts an initial value.
- `act` is exported from `react`.

### Upgrade path

Upgrade to 18.3 first (it logs deprecation warnings), then run the official codemods (`npx codemod react/19/migration-recipe`).

topics.title: React Server Components Overview
topics.summary: Server Components render on the server and send results to the client without shipping their JavaScript.
topics.description:
**React Server Components (RSC)** are components that run **only on the server** (at build time or per request). They can access databases, file systems and secrets directly, and send their rendered output to the browser as a special serialized stream, **without adding their code to the client bundle**.

### Server vs Client components

| | Server Component (default in Next.js App Router) | Client Component (`"use client"`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Runs | server only | server (SSR) + browser |
| State/effects | no `useState`, `useEffect` | yes |
| Event handlers | no | yes |
| Async/await | **yes**, components can be `async` | no (use `use`) |
| Browser APIs | no | yes |
| Bundle size | zero | counted |

### Example

```jsx
// app/page.jsx - Server Component
export default async function Page() {
  const products = await db.product.findMany();   // direct DB access
  return (
    <>
      <ProductList products={products} />
      <AddToCartButton />      {/* a Client Component */}
    </>
  );
}
```

### Key rules

- `"use client"` at the top of a file marks a **boundary**; everything imported into it is client code.
- Server Components can render Client Components, and pass **serializable props** (no functions).
- Client Components can render Server Components only through `children` props.
- Use `"use server"` for Server Actions.

### Benefits

Smaller bundles, no client waterfalls (fetch near the data), better security for secrets, and streaming UI with Suspense.

### Not the same as SSR

SSR renders HTML on the server for first load, but all components still ship and hydrate. RSC components never hydrate.

topics.title: Next.js Overview: App Router, SSR, SSG, ISR
topics.summary: Next.js is the main React framework: routing, rendering strategies, data fetching, and deployment built in.
topics.description:
**Next.js** (by Vercel) is a full-stack React framework. It adds what plain React lacks: file-based routing, server rendering, API routes, image and font optimization, caching and bundling.

### App Router (`app/` directory)

- **File-based routes:** `app/blog/[slug]/page.jsx` -> `/blog/hello`.
- Special files: `layout.jsx` (shared, persistent UI), `loading.jsx` (Suspense fallback), `error.jsx` (error boundary), `not-found.jsx`, `route.js` (API endpoints), `middleware.js`.
- Components are **Server Components** by default; add `"use client"` for interactivity.
- **Server Actions** for mutations; **Route Handlers** for REST endpoints.

### Rendering strategies

| Strategy | When HTML is made | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **SSG** (static) | build time | marketing, docs, blogs |
| **SSR** (dynamic) | each request | personalized or always-fresh pages |
| **ISR** | build, then revalidated in the background after N seconds or on demand | catalogs, news |
| **CSR** | in the browser | dashboards behind login |
| **PPR / streaming** | static shell + dynamic holes | mixed pages |

Pages are static by default; using `cookies()`, `headers()`, or `cache: "no-store"` makes them dynamic. `generateStaticParams` pre-renders dynamic routes.

### Data fetching & caching

Use `async` Server Components with `fetch`. Control freshness with `next: { revalidate: 60 }`, tags (`revalidateTag`) or `revalidatePath`. Caching defaults changed in v15, so check the docs of your version.

### Extras

`next/image`, `next/font`, `next/link` (prefetching), metadata API for SEO, Turbopack, edge runtime, environment variables (`NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix reaches the browser).

### When to choose it

SEO-critical, content-heavy or full-stack apps. For a pure client dashboard, Vite + React is simpler. Alternatives: React Router v7 framework mode, Remix, Astro, TanStack Start.

topics.title: TypeScript: Typing Props, State and Events
topics.summary: Type props with interfaces, let TypeScript infer state, and use React's built-in event and element types.
topics.description:
TypeScript catches mistakes (wrong prop, missing field, undefined access) before you run the code. Create a project with `npm create vite@latest app -- --template react-ts`. Component files use `.tsx`.

### Props

```tsx
interface ButtonProps {
  label: string;
  variant?: "primary" | "ghost";          // optional + union
  onClick: (id: number) => void;           // function type
  children?: React.ReactNode;              // anything renderable
}
function Button({ label, variant = "primary", onClick }: ButtonProps) { ... }
```

Prefer `interface`/`type` plus a plain function. `React.FC` is optional and no longer recommended by default.

### Useful prop helpers

- `React.ComponentProps<"button">` - all native props of an element.
- `extends React.ButtonHTMLAttributes<HTMLButtonElement>` to forward native props.
- `React.ReactNode` for children, `React.ReactElement` for a single element.
- `React.CSSProperties` for style objects.

### Hooks

- `useState<User | null>(null)` - give a generic when the initial value does not describe the full type.
- `useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)` for DOM refs; `useRef<number>(0)` for mutable values.
- `useReducer` with a **discriminated union** for actions.
- `useContext` with a context created as `createContext<Ctx | null>(null)` and a hook that narrows the null.

### Events

```tsx
const onChange = (e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => setName(e.target.value);
const onSubmit = (e: React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) => { e.preventDefault(); };
const onClick = (e: React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) => {};
```

Tip: write the handler inline and hover to see the inferred type, or use `React.ChangeEventHandler<HTMLInputElement>`.
keyPoints: Props via interface/type; mark optional with ?
Use unions for variant-style props
useState generics when the initial value is null or empty

pitfalls: Using any to silence errors instead of modeling data.
useState([]) infers never[]; give an explicit type.

interview.a: It is optional and no longer recommended by default; plain functions with typed props are simpler and handle generics and children more explicitly.

interview.q: How do you type a ref to an input?
interview.a: useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null), then access ref.current?.focus().

topics.title: Project Architecture: Feature Folders and Absolute Imports
topics.summary: Organize code by feature, keep shared code separate, and use path aliases to avoid ../../../ imports.
topics.description:
There is no official structure, but a good one keeps related code together and makes dependencies clear.

### Folder by type (small apps)

```
src/
  components/  hooks/  pages/  services/  utils/  context/
```

Simple, but as the app grows, one feature's files are scattered across the tree.

### Folder by feature (recommended for growth)

```
src/
  app/            # providers, router, store setup
  features/
    auth/
      components/ hooks/ api.ts types.ts index.ts
    cart/
      components/ cartSlice.ts index.ts
  components/     # shared, generic UI (Button, Modal)
  hooks/          # shared hooks
  lib/            # axios instance, query client
  pages/ (or routes/)
  assets/ styles/
```

### Rules that keep it healthy

- A feature exposes a **public API** via `index.ts`; other features import only from it.
- Features do not import from each other's internals; shared code goes down to `components/`, `lib/`.
- **Colocate** tests, styles and stories next to components (`Button/Button.tsx`, `Button.test.tsx`).
- Keep pages thin: they compose feature components.
- Put API calls in `api` files, not inside JSX.

### Absolute imports (aliases)

Replace `../../../components/Button` with `@/components/Button`.

```js
// vite.config.js
resolve: { alias: { "@": fileURLToPath(new URL("./src", import.meta.url)) } }
```

```json
// tsconfig.json / jsconfig.json
{ "compilerOptions": { "baseUrl": ".", "paths": { "@/*": ["src/*"] } } }
```

### Don't over-engineer

Start flat and refactor when a folder gets crowded. Copying a huge enterprise structure into a todo app slows you down.

Shared UI and utilities live outside features

topics.title: Environment Variables in React
topics.summary: Configure API URLs and keys per environment with .env files, remembering that front-end env vars are public.
topics.description:
Different environments (development, staging, production) need different settings such as API URLs. Use **environment variables** instead of hard-coding.

### Vite

- Create `.env`, `.env.development`, `.env.production`, `.env.local` (git-ignored).
- Only variables prefixed with **`VITE_`** are exposed to the client.
- Read with `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL`. Built-ins: `import.meta.env.MODE`, `DEV`, `PROD`, `BASE_URL`.
- Restart the dev server after changing a `.env` file.

```
# .env.development
VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:4000
# .env.production
VITE_API_URL=https://api.example.com
```

### Create React App / Next.js

CRA used `process.env.REACT_APP_*`. Next.js exposes `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` to the browser; other variables stay on the server.

### Critical: they are not secret

Variables are **inlined into the JavaScript bundle at build time**, so anyone can read them in DevTools. Never put private API keys, database URLs or tokens in client env variables. Keep secrets on a backend (or Server Components / API routes) and call that.

### Practices

- Commit a `.env.example` with variable names but no real values.
- Do not commit `.env.local` or `.env.production` with secrets.
- Validate at startup (for example with Zod) and fail fast on missing values.
- On CI/hosting (Vercel, Netlify) define variables in the dashboard; they apply at **build** time for static builds.
- For runtime config on one image, load a `/config.json` at start or inject through a server.

Read via import.meta.env
Client env vars are public in the bundle
Commit .env.example, never secrets
Static builds read variables at build time

Changing .env without restarting the dev server.

interview.a: They are replaced with their values in the built JavaScript, so any user can see them in the browser.

interview.q: How do you keep real secrets safe in a React app?
interview.a: Keep them on a server or serverless backend and have the front end call that API; never ship them in client code.

topics.title: ESLint and Prettier
topics.summary: ESLint finds bugs and bad patterns; Prettier formats code automatically; together they keep a codebase consistent.
topics.description:
### ESLint - code quality

ESLint analyzes code and reports problems. Vite templates include a flat config (`eslint.config.js`) with:

- **`eslint-plugin-react-hooks`** - `rules-of-hooks` (error) and `exhaustive-deps` (warn). Essential.
- **`eslint-plugin-react-refresh`** - keeps fast refresh working.
- **`typescript-eslint`** for TS projects.
- **`eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y`** - accessibility checks.
- **`eslint-plugin-react-compiler`** (or compiler rules in react-hooks) - flags code the compiler cannot optimize.

Run `npm run lint`, and fix automatically with `eslint --fix`.

### Prettier - formatting

Prettier is an opinionated formatter: line length, quotes, semicolons, trailing commas. It ends style arguments in code reviews. Config in `.prettierrc`:

```json
{ "semi": true, "singleQuote": false, "printWidth": 100, "trailingComma": "all" }
```

Add `eslint-config-prettier` so ESLint does not fight Prettier about formatting.

### Editor and team workflow

- Enable **format on save** in VS Code.
- Add scripts: `"lint"`, `"format": "prettier --write ."`.
- Use **husky + lint-staged** to run linters on staged files before each commit.
- Run lint, type-check (`tsc --noEmit`) and tests in **CI**.
- Add `.editorconfig` for tabs/spaces across editors.

### Alternative

**Biome** is a fast single tool that does both linting and formatting.

react-hooks plugin catches hook mistakes
eslint-config-prettier avoids rule conflicts
husky + lint-staged enforce checks on commit
Run lint, types and tests in CI

Configuring ESLint style rules that conflict with Prettier.

interview.q: What does the exhaustive-deps rule do?
interview.a: It warns when an effect, memo or callback uses a reactive value that is missing from its dependency array, preventing stale closures.

interview.q: ESLint vs Prettier?
interview.a: ESLint finds code-quality problems and risky patterns; Prettier only formats code consistently. They are complementary.

topics.title: Project: Todo App
topics.summary: The classic first React project: add, toggle, edit, delete and filter todos.
topics.description:
A Todo app exercises almost every beginner concept: state, lists with keys, controlled inputs, events, derived data and conditional rendering.

### Features to build

- Add a todo with Enter or the Add button (ignore blank text).
- Toggle done, delete, and edit text inline.
- Filter: **All / Active / Done**.
- Show the count of remaining items and a **Clear completed** button.

### Design decisions

- State: `todos` array of `{ id, text, done }`, plus `filter` string and the input `text`. The **visible list** and **remaining count** are *derived*, not stored.
- Use stable ids (`crypto.randomUUID()` or an incrementing counter), never the array index as key.
- Update immutably with `map` and `filter`.
- Extract `TodoItem` to keep the main component small.

### Next steps

1. Persist to `localStorage` with the `useLocalStorage` hook.
2. Move logic into `useReducer`.
3. Add drag-and-drop ordering.
4. Sync with a backend using TanStack Query.
5. Write RTL tests for add, toggle and filter.

Derive visible list and counts
Use stable ids as keys
Immutable updates with map/filter
Extract TodoItem; persist as a next step
pitfalls: Using the array index as id after deletions.
Storing remaining count in state.

interview.q: Which parts of the todo app should not be stored in state?
interview.a: The filtered list and the remaining count, because they can be derived from the todos and filter during render.

interview.q: How would you persist todos across reloads?
interview.a: Initialize state lazily from localStorage and write it back in an effect when todos change, ideally through a useLocalStorage hook.

topics.title: Project: Counter with Undo/Redo (useReducer)
topics.summary: Build a counter whose history is managed by a reducer, enabling undo and redo.
topics.description:
A plain counter is easy; adding **undo/redo** shows why `useReducer` shines: all transitions live in one pure function, and history is just data.

### The history shape

```js
{ past: [0, 1, 2], present: 3, future: [] }
```

- **Change** (`inc`, `dec`, `set`): push `present` onto `past`, set the new `present`, **clear `future`**.
- **Undo**: move the last item of `past` into `present`, and push the old `present` onto the front of `future`.
- **Redo**: the reverse of undo.
- **Reset**: back to the initial state (and clear history).

### Why this works

State is immutable and each action returns a new object, so snapshots are cheap and safe. The same pattern powers text editors, drawing apps, and form builders. Libraries like `use-undo` and Redux's `redux-undo` implement it.

### UI details

- Disable Undo when `past` is empty, Redo when `future` is empty.
- Show history length for learning purposes.
- Keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z) can be added with an effect.

### Extension ideas

Limit history to 20 steps, add a step size, or persist the reducer state.
keyPoints: History = { past, present, future }
Any new change clears the future
Undo/redo just move values between lists
Pure reducers make time travel easy
Disable buttons when stacks are empty
pitfalls: Mutating the past array with push.
Forgetting to clear future after a new change.

examples.title: Counter with undo/redo

interview.q: Why is a reducer a good fit for undo/redo?
interview.a: Each action returns a new immutable state, so keeping past and future snapshots is simple and all transitions are in one testable function.

interview.q: What happens to the future stack after a new change?
interview.a: It is cleared, because the redo history no longer applies once the timeline branches.

topics.title: Project: Accessible Tabs
topics.summary: Build a tab component with ARIA roles and keyboard navigation.
topics.description:
Tabs are a staple UI widget. A good implementation is also a lesson in accessibility.

### Structure

- A container with `role="tablist"` holding buttons with `role="tab"`.
- Each tab has `aria-selected` and `aria-controls` (id of its panel).
- Each panel has `role="tabpanel"` and `aria-labelledby` pointing to its tab.
- Only the active tab is in the **tab order** (`tabIndex={0}`); the others use `-1` (the "roving tabindex").

### Keyboard behavior (WAI-ARIA pattern)

- **ArrowRight / ArrowLeft** move to the next/previous tab (wrapping around) and activate it.
- **Home / End** jump to the first/last tab.
- **Tab** moves focus from the tab list into the panel.

### State

A single piece of state: `active` index (or id). Render only the active panel, or render all and hide with `hidden` if you want to preserve inner state.

### Make it data-driven

Pass an array of `{ id, label, content }` so adding a tab needs no new JSX. Later convert to the compound component pattern (`Tabs.List`, `Tabs.Tab`).

### Styling

Use an underline or background to show the active tab; keep a visible focus ring.
keyPoints: State is the active tab index
roles: tablist, tab, tabpanel with aria-selected/controls
Roving tabindex: only the active tab is tabbable
Arrow keys, Home, End move between tabs
Data-driven array of tabs
pitfalls: Using only mouse handlers so keyboard users are blocked.
Unmounting panels when you need to preserve their form state.

examples.title: Tabs with keyboard navigation

interview.q: What is a roving tabindex?
interview.a: Only the active item has tabIndex 0 and the others -1, so Tab enters the widget once and arrow keys move among its items.

interview.q: Which ARIA roles make a tab widget accessible?
interview.a: tablist for the container, tab for each tab and tabpanel for each panel, linked by aria-controls and aria-labelledby.

topics.title: Project: Accordion
topics.summary: Build a collapsible FAQ where one or many sections can be open at a time.
topics.description:
An accordion shows a list of headings; clicking one reveals its content. It is a perfect lesson in lifted state and accessibility.

### State design

- **Single-open mode:** `openId` (or `null`). Clicking the open one closes it.
- **Multi-open mode:** a `Set`/array of open ids, or a boolean per item.
- Keep the state in the **parent** `Accordion` so it can enforce "only one open".

### Accessibility

- Each header is a real `<button>` inside a heading (`<h3>`).
- `aria-expanded` on the button; `aria-controls` points to the panel id.
- The panel has `role="region"` and `aria-labelledby`.
- Hide closed panels with the `hidden` attribute (removes from the tab order and accessibility tree).

### Animation

Animating height needs care: use CSS grid trick `grid-template-rows: 0fr -> 1fr` with a transition, or the native `<details>`/`<summary>` element, which gives toggling and keyboard support for free (and `name` attribute for exclusive groups).

### Design as data

Render from an array: `items.map(item => <AccordionItem ... />)`.

### Extension ideas

Controlled/uncontrolled modes, icons that rotate, deep linking via the URL hash.
keyPoints: State: openId (single) or a set of ids (multiple)
Use buttons inside headings with aria-expanded
hidden attribute keeps closed panels out of tab order
Render from a data array
Native <details> is a good alternative
pitfalls: Making the header a div with onClick.
Keeping state in every item so the group cannot enforce one-open.

examples.title: FAQ accordion with single/multiple modes

interview.q: How do you make an accordion accessible?
interview.a: Use buttons for the headers with aria-expanded and aria-controls, give panels role region with aria-labelledby, and hide closed panels with the hidden attribute.

interview.q: Where should the open state live for a one-at-a-time accordion?
interview.a: In the parent Accordion, so it can close other items when one opens.

topics.title: Project: Accessible Modal Dialog
topics.summary: A modal rendered in a portal with Escape to close, focus trap, scroll lock and focus restoration.
topics.description:
A production-quality modal is more than a centered div. It must:

1. **Render in a portal** (`createPortal` to `document.body`) to avoid clipping and z-index problems.
2. Have `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal="true"` and a label (`aria-labelledby` the title).
3. **Move focus** into the dialog when it opens.
4. **Trap focus**: Tab and Shift+Tab cycle within the dialog.
5. Close on **Escape** and on **backdrop click**.
6. **Lock page scroll** while open.
7. **Restore focus** to the element that opened it on close.

### Implementation tips

- Remember the previously focused element (`document.activeElement`) in a ref when opening.
- Store the `onClose` callback in a ref (or `useCallback` in the parent). Otherwise an inline arrow function changes every render, the effect re-runs and **steals focus again**.
- Clean up everything in the effect cleanup (listener, body overflow, focus).
- `backdrop onClick` closes, but `dialog onClick` calls `stopPropagation`.

### Native alternative

The HTML `<dialog>` element with `showModal()` provides focus trapping, Escape handling, backdrop and top-layer rendering built in. In React, call `ref.current.showModal()` in an effect. Many libraries (Radix Dialog, Headless UI) wrap these concerns for you.
keyPoints: Portal + role="dialog" + aria-modal
Focus in on open, trapped inside, restored on close
Escape and backdrop click close it
Lock body scroll while open
Keep callbacks in refs to avoid re-running effects
pitfalls: Not restoring focus to the trigger button.
An effect depending on an inline onClose that re-focuses on every render.

examples.title: Modal with focus trap and focus restore

interview.q: What makes a modal accessible?
interview.a: role=dialog with aria-modal and a label, focus moved in and trapped, Escape to close, scroll lock, and focus restored to the trigger on close.

interview.q: Why use a portal for modals?
interview.a: It renders the modal at the top level of the DOM so parent overflow, transforms or z-index cannot clip or hide it.

topics.title: Project: Search, Filter and Sort a List
topics.summary: Filter a list by text and category, sort it, and highlight results using derived data.
topics.description:
Search UIs are everywhere: product lists, user directories, docs. The key lesson is **derived state**: keep the *inputs* in state and compute the *result* during render.

### State

- `query` (string)
- `category` (string)
- `sort` ("name" | "price")

### Derived result

```js
const results = useMemo(() => {
  const q = query.trim().toLowerCase();
  return PRODUCTS
    .filter(p => (category === "all" || p.category === category))
    .filter(p => p.name.toLowerCase().includes(q))
    .sort(sortFns[sort]);          // sort a copy or after filter (filter makes a new array)
}, [query, category, sort]);
```

### UX details

- Show the **result count** and an **empty state** ("No products match 'xyz'") with a Clear button.
- Normalize text: lowercase, trim; for accent-insensitive search use `normalize("NFD")`.
- Highlight matches by splitting the text on the query.
- For very large lists debounce the query (next projects) or use `useDeferredValue`.
- Keep filters in the **URL** (`useSearchParams`) so results are shareable.

### Performance

For a few thousand items plain filtering is fine. Use `useMemo` only when it is measurably slow. For huge data, filter on the server.
keyPoints: Inputs in state; results are derived
Normalize text for matching
Show count and an empty state
Highlight matches with a small helper
Consider URL state and debouncing
pitfalls: Storing the filtered list in state and trying to keep it synced.
Sorting the original array in place with sort().

examples.title: Product search with category and sort

interview.q: Why compute the filtered list instead of storing it in state?
interview.a: It is derived from the query, category and data; storing it would duplicate data and risk it getting out of sync.

interview.q: Why is calling sort directly on a state array a bug?
interview.a: sort mutates the array in place, violating immutability; sort a copy or a freshly filtered array.

topics.title: Project: Pagination Component
topics.summary: A reusable pagination control with page numbers, ellipses and a page-size selector.
topics.description:
Build pagination as a **reusable, presentational component** driven by props, with the page state kept in the parent.

### Props

`page`, `pageSize`, `total`, `onPageChange`, optionally `siblings` (how many neighbors to show).

### The math

```js
const totalPages = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(total / pageSize));
const start = (page - 1) * pageSize;
const slice = items.slice(start, start + pageSize);
```

### Page number window with ellipsis

For 20 pages, with the current page 10, show: `1 ... 9 10 11 ... 20`. A helper generates an array of numbers and `"..."` markers: always show first and last page, the current page, its siblings, and an ellipsis when there is a gap.

### Edge cases to handle

- Clamp `page` when `pageSize` or `total` changes (if you change page size to 50 while on page 9, jump back to a valid page - often page 1).
- Disable Prev on page 1 and Next on the last page.
- Mark the current page with `aria-current="page"` and wrap the buttons in a `<nav aria-label="Pagination">`.

### Server-side

With an API, send `page` and `limit`, and read `total` from the response. Put `page` in the URL for shareable links and back-button support.
keyPoints: Compute totalPages with Math.ceil
Slice data with (page - 1) * pageSize
Generate numbers with ellipses around the current page
Reset or clamp page when page size changes
aria-current="page" and a nav landmark
pitfalls: Staying on page 9 after changing the page size, showing an empty page.
Off-by-one errors in the start index.

examples.title: Pagination with ellipsis and page size

interview.q: How do you calculate the items for page N?
interview.a: start = (N - 1) * pageSize and take items.slice(start, start + pageSize); totalPages = Math.ceil(total / pageSize).

interview.q: What should happen when the page size changes?
interview.a: Reset or clamp the current page so it still exists, typically setting page to 1.

topics.title: Project: Star Rating
topics.summary: An interactive rating widget with hover preview, click to set, and keyboard accessibility.
topics.description:
A star rating shows how to combine **two pieces of state** (the saved value and the hover preview) and derive what to display.

### State

- `rating` - the committed value (0 means none).
- `hover` - the value being previewed while the mouse is over a star (0 when not hovering).
- Display value: `const shown = hover || rating;`

### Interactions

- `onMouseEnter` on star `n` -> `setHover(n)`.
- `onMouseLeave` on the container -> `setHover(0)`.
- `onClick` -> `setRating(n)`; clicking the same star again can clear the rating.
- **Keyboard & a11y:** use real buttons (focusable), `role="radiogroup"` with `role="radio"` and `aria-checked`, `aria-label="3 stars"`. Arrow keys can change the value.

### Rendering stars

`Array.from({ length: max }, (_, i) => i + 1).map(n => ...)`. A star is filled if `n <= shown`. Use a text star (`★` / `☆`) or inline SVG; no images are needed.

### Make it reusable

topics.title: Project: Theme Switcher with Context
topics.summary: A light/dark/system theme provider that persists the choice and follows the OS preference.
topics.description:
This project combines **Context**, **custom hooks**, **effects**, **localStorage** and **CSS variables**.

### Requirements

- Three modes: `light`, `dark`, `system`.
- The `system` mode follows `prefers-color-scheme` and updates live when the OS setting changes.
- The choice is saved in `localStorage`.
- Any component can read or change the theme via `useTheme()`.

### Design

1. `ThemeProvider` holds `mode` state (initialized lazily from storage, default `system`).
2. A derived `resolved` value (`light` or `dark`) is computed: if mode is `system`, use the `matchMedia` result.
3. An effect subscribes to the media query (`mq.addEventListener("change", ...)`) and cleans up.
4. Another effect writes the choice to storage and sets `data-theme` on an element (or `document.documentElement`).
5. `useTheme()` throws if used outside the provider.

### CSS

Define colors as CSS variables under `[data-theme="dark"]`. All components just use `var(--bg)`, so changing the attribute restyles everything without re-rendering them.

### Pitfalls to avoid

- Flash of the wrong theme at page load: set the attribute with a tiny inline script in `index.html`.
- Memoize the context value so consumers do not re-render needlessly.
- Guard `localStorage` and `matchMedia` access (SSR, private mode).

topics.title: Project: Shopping Cart with useReducer
topics.summary: A cart with add, increment, decrement, remove and totals, managed by a reducer.
topics.description:
A cart is the textbook case for `useReducer`: several actions, each with clear rules, operating on the same list.

### State shape

```js
items: [{ id, name, price, qty }]
```

Store **ids and quantities**, and derive totals. Never store `total` in state.

### Actions

| Action | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `add` | if the product exists, qty + 1; otherwise append with qty 1 |
| `inc` / `dec` | change qty; when qty reaches 0 remove the item |
| `remove` | delete the line |
| `clear` | empty the cart |

### Derived values

```js
const count = items.reduce((n, i) => n + i.qty, 0);
const total = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0);
```

### Real-world considerations

- **Money:** store prices in the smallest unit (paise/cents as integers) to avoid floating-point errors (`0.1 + 0.2`). Format with `Intl.NumberFormat`.
- **Context:** expose the cart via `CartProvider` + `useCart()` so the header badge and product list share it.
- **Persistence:** save to `localStorage` or the server for logged-in users.
- **Validation:** the server must recompute prices; never trust client totals.
- **Stock limits:** cap qty at available stock.

interview.a: Floating point numbers cannot represent many decimals exactly, so use the smallest currency unit (cents or paise) and format only for display.

interview.a: They can be computed from the items, so storing them would duplicate data and risk inconsistency.

topics.title: Project: Stopwatch with Laps
topics.summary: A stopwatch using setInterval, refs for timer ids and Date.now for accuracy.
topics.description:
A stopwatch teaches timers, cleanup and why refs are useful.

### Naive vs accurate

Counting `+10ms` every 10 ms tick drifts because `setInterval` is not precise (tabs in the background are throttled to 1 s or more). The accurate way is to store a **start timestamp** and compute elapsed time from the clock on every tick:

```js
elapsed = accumulated + (Date.now() - startedAt)
```

`performance.now()` is better for monotonic time.

### State and refs

- `running` (boolean) and `elapsed` (ms) are **state** because they affect the UI.
- The interval id and `startedAt` live in a **ref** (changing them should not re-render).
- `laps` array in state.

### Start / Stop / Reset

- **Start:** record `startedAt = Date.now() - elapsed`, create the interval that sets `elapsed`.
- **Stop:** clear the interval.
- **Reset:** stop, set elapsed to 0, clear laps.
- **Lap:** push the current elapsed time (and delta from the previous lap).

### Cleanup

Return `clearInterval` from the effect so the timer stops when the component unmounts or `running` becomes false. Run the interval from a `useEffect` that depends on `running`.

### Formatting

`mm:ss.cs` using `padStart(2, "0")`. Use tabular numbers (`font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums`) so digits do not jitter.

topics.title: Project: Multi-step Form Wizard
topics.summary: A step-by-step form with per-step validation, back/next navigation and a review step.
topics.description:
Long forms are friendlier as wizards. The challenge is **state across steps** and **validation per step**.

### Architecture

- One parent `Wizard` owns the **entire form data** object and the `step` index.
- Each step component receives `data`, `onChange` and `errors` (presentational).
- The parent validates only the **current step** on Next; a final submit validates everything again.

### Key decisions

- **Keep all data in the parent** so going Back does not lose input.
- A `steps` array describing `{ title, fields, validate }` keeps the navigation generic.
- Show a **progress indicator** (Step 2 of 4) and mark completed steps.
- Last step is a **review/summary** with edit links that jump to a step.
- Disable the submit button while submitting; show success/failure state.

### Accessibility and UX

- Move focus to the step heading (or the first error) when the step changes.
- Announce errors with `role="alert"`.
- Use proper labels, `autocomplete` attributes and input types (`email`, `tel`).

### Going further

- Persist drafts in `localStorage` so users can resume.
- Put the step in the URL (`/signup/step-2`) so refresh and browser back work.
- For big forms use React Hook Form with a single `useForm` across steps and `trigger(["fieldA"])` for step validation.
- Model the flow as a state machine (XState) for branching steps.

topics.title: Project: Debounced Search with Race Protection
topics.summary: Combine useDebounce, simulated async search, loading states and stale-response protection.
topics.description:
This project ties together custom hooks, effects, cleanup and async states - a typical interview task.

### Flow

1. User types -> `query` updates instantly (controlled input).
2. `useDebounce(query, 400)` produces `debouncedQuery`.
3. An effect depends on `debouncedQuery`: if empty, clear results; otherwise start a request.
4. The effect cleanup marks the request as stale (`ignore = true` or `AbortController`).
5. UI shows **idle**, **loading**, **error**, **empty**, and **results** states.

### Why both debounce and cancellation

- **Debounce** reduces the number of requests.
- **Cancellation/ignore** guarantees a slow earlier response never overwrites a newer one.

### Details

- Trim the query and ignore queries shorter than 2 characters.
- Keep previous results visible while loading a new query (less flicker).
- Show the number of requests made to see debouncing working.
- Cache results by query in a `useRef(new Map())` to avoid repeated calls.
- Handle errors with a retry option; surface them with `role="alert"`.

### Production

In real apps use TanStack Query: `useQuery({ queryKey: ["search", debounced], queryFn, enabled: debounced.length > 1 })` gives caching, cancellation and states for free.

topics.title: Project: Infinite Scroll with IntersectionObserver
topics.summary: Load more items automatically when a sentinel element scrolls into view.
topics.description:
Infinite scroll appends content as the user nears the bottom. The modern way uses **`IntersectionObserver`** instead of listening to every scroll event.

### The idea

1. Render the list and a small **sentinel** element after the last item.
2. Observe the sentinel with `IntersectionObserver`.
3. When it intersects the viewport (or the scroll container, via `root`), call `loadMore()`.
4. Append the new page; the sentinel moves down and the cycle repeats.

### Implementation details

- Store `items`, `loading`, and `hasMore` in state.
- Create the observer in a `useEffect` that depends on `loading` and `hasMore`; **disconnect** it in cleanup. Re-creating the observer after each load also re-checks visibility when the new page is short.
- Use `rootMargin: "200px"` to start loading before the user hits the bottom.
- Prevent duplicate loads with the `loading` guard.
- When there is no more data, stop observing and show "You reached the end".

### Accessibility and UX

- Provide a **Load more** button as a fallback (also helps keyboard users and reaching the footer).
- Announce loaded content with `aria-live="polite"`.
- For thousands of items combine with virtualization.
- Preserve scroll position when navigating back (store pages in a cache like TanStack Query's `useInfiniteQuery`).

### Production note

`useInfiniteQuery` from TanStack Query manages pages, cursors and `fetchNextPage` for you, leaving only the observer to write.

topics.title: Building and Deploying a React App
topics.summary: Build static files with Vite and host them anywhere, remembering the SPA fallback and base path.
topics.description:
A client-side React app is just **static files**: one `index.html`, hashed JS and CSS bundles and assets. Deployment means building them and serving them over HTTPS.

### Build

`npm run build` runs `vite build`, creating a `dist/` folder with minified, tree-shaken, code-split and **content-hashed** files (for example `index-8f3a2c.js`). Hashes allow aggressive caching: set `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` for `/assets/*` and **no-cache** for `index.html`.

### Preview before shipping

`npm run preview` serves `dist/` locally. Test the production build, not just the dev server.

### Two classic gotchas

1. **SPA fallback.** With React Router, `/dashboard` is not a real file. The host must serve `index.html` for unknown paths, otherwise a refresh gives 404 (see Vercel/Netlify topic, Nginx `try_files`).
2. **Base path.** If the site lives at `https://user.github.io/my-repo/`, set `base: "/my-repo/"` in `vite.config.js` (and `basename` in the router).

### Hosting options

| Type | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Static hosts / CDNs | Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, GitHub Pages, S3 + CloudFront, Firebase Hosting |
| Containers | Docker + Nginx on any cloud |
| Node/SSR | Next.js on Vercel, Node servers |

### Production checklist

- Environment variables set for the production build.
- HTTPS, compression (Brotli/gzip) and a CDN.
- Error monitoring (Sentry) with source maps uploaded privately.
- Analytics and Web Vitals.
- CI pipeline: install, lint, type-check, test, build, deploy previews for pull requests.

Vercel and Netlify are the easiest ways to publish a React app. Both integrate with GitHub/GitLab: every push builds and deploys, and every pull request gets a **preview URL**.

### Steps (both platforms)

1. Push your project to GitHub.
2. Import the repository on the platform.
3. Framework preset: **Vite**. Build command `npm run build`, output directory `dist`.
4. Add **environment variables** in the dashboard (they are used at build time).
5. Deploy. You get an HTTPS URL; add a custom domain and DNS records.

### SPA routing

- **Vercel:** add `vercel.json` with a rewrite to `/index.html` (Next.js needs nothing).
- **Netlify:** add `public/_redirects` containing `/* /index.html 200`, or `netlify.toml`.

| Feature | Vercel | Netlify |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Preview deployments | yes | yes |
| Serverless functions | `api/` folder | `netlify/functions` |
| Edge functions / middleware | yes | yes |
| Forms, identity | - | built-in forms |
| Rollbacks | instant, one click | instant, one click |

### Tips

- Set `NODE_VERSION` to match local development.
- Never commit `.env` secrets; use the dashboard.
- For secrets (API keys), call a serverless function from the front end.
- Use branch deploys for staging, main for production.
- Watch build logs: case-sensitive imports (`Button.jsx` vs `button.jsx`) work on Windows/macOS but fail on Linux builds.

topics.title: SEO for React Apps
topics.summary: Client-rendered SPAs are hard for crawlers; use SSR/SSG, proper metadata, and sitemaps for content that must rank.
topics.description:
A plain Vite React app ships an almost empty HTML file and builds the page with JavaScript. Google can run JavaScript but with delay and limits, and many other crawlers and social previews (WhatsApp, X, LinkedIn) **do not**. So for public content pages, SEO needs extra work.

### Options (from simplest to strongest)

1. **Better metadata in CSR:** per-page `<title>` and `<meta>` with `react-helmet-async` (or React 19 native `<title>`). Works for Google eventually, not for social previews.
2. **Prerendering / static generation:** generate HTML for each route at build time (`vite-plugin-ssr`/Vike, `react-snap`, Astro, Next.js SSG). Great for blogs and docs.
3. **SSR (server-side rendering):** the server returns full HTML per request. Next.js, Remix/React Router framework mode, TanStack Start.
4. **Hybrid:** SSR/SSG for marketing pages and CSR for the logged-in app. Many companies split `www` from `app`.

### Checklist

- Unique `<title>` (under about 60 chars) and meta `description` per page.
- Semantic HTML: one `h1`, headings in order, real `<a href>` links for navigation (crawlers follow anchors, not onClick).
- Open Graph and Twitter card tags for sharing.
- `canonical` link, `robots.txt` and `sitemap.xml`.
- Proper **status codes** (a client-rendered 404 page still returns 200 - a "soft 404").
- Structured data (JSON-LD).
- Fast Core Web Vitals; image `alt` text.
- Avoid content that only appears after interaction.

### Test

Use "View Source", Google Search Console's URL Inspection, and the Rich Results Test.
